subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
That this House is of the opinion that Canada urgently needs a new national transportation policy, aimed at removing regional inequalities and disparities, and including amongst other things the equalizing of the freight rate structure, the discontinuance of the practice of abandoning railway lines and services, and the greater use of the ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am extremely happy to move this motion today in view of what has occurred in the last several days, and in view of the scheduled conference between the four western premiers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who is also in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, has been butting in, and, as I understand, he has unfortunately been given some authority in arranging this meeting. I will get into that matter in a few minutes.
To begin with, I want to repeat what we on this side of the House have said every year for many years, namely that Canada needs a new transportation policy. In fact, we have needed one for decades. Successive Liberal and Tory
Transportation Policy
governments in Ottawa have failed miserably over those same decades to see to it that Canada had a transportation system which was not only efficient but which was integrated and fair in collecting the costs of transportation from Canadian consumers wherever they lived in this country. This new transportation policy must include a principle overriding all others, that transportation is a public utility; that the purpose of our railways, our airlines, our pipelines and our communications systems is to provide fast and efficient service-with emphasis on the word "service"-and that profit must be secondary. Because these transportation systems are essential public services, essential to our well-being as a nation, it therefore logically follows, I submit, that they should be publicly owned and controlled.
Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party, and in the CCF years before, have always advocated that our railway systems, airlines systems, pipelines and telecommunications systems should be publicy owned and treated as public utilities. They are no different in terms of their essential public service; there is no difference between them and our streets, sidewalks, sewer and water systems and the publicly owned telephone systems that we have in western Canada. Because of the very nature of their operations, they should be publicly owned and controlled.
Private profit from essential public services can no longer be allowed to take precedence over the requirements of our country for transportation and communication services. I submit that the profit motive has no place in the operations of the railway, airline or telecommunication systems or pipelines, in the same way as the profit motive has no place in the operations of a sewer and water systems or our streets and sidewalks. Anybody who suggested that there should be a profit motive in the operation of these public services would be laughed out of town I am sure.
That is the basic tenet of what we submit, and have submitted for years, in terms of what should be contained in a new national transportation policy. A national transportation policy must provide for the operation of the services and take into account our geography, climate and scattered population. We need a government in Canada which, in devising a national transportation policy, will remind itself that there are people and places in Canada besides Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, that there are millions of people in those places who are entitled to equal and fair treatment and to good service from our transportation system.
Mr. Speaker, there have been arguments put forward and anger exhibited in this House ever since 1885 about discriminatory freight rates. I will assume for the time being that the motivation of the Prime Minister and the government is very high in arranging a meeting with the four western premiers to discuss the problems of western Canada, one of which will be transportation and, in particular, rail transportation. There is no reason in the world why the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) cannot present concrete proposals to the four western premiers on a revised national transportation policy, and specific proposals on what the government would like to do about freight rates.

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
In a speech I made a couple of months ago in the House I gave examples of what we mean by discrimination in the area of transportation in Canada. I want to cite more examples. It seems to me that we have had a great deal of difficulty in convincing governments, made up of either one of the two major parties, of the difficulties in this area. As well, we must contend with the appalling lack of understanding and knowledge of this matter on the part of people generally in central Canada. The idea that our present rate structure is justified because of the existence of the Panama Canal is surely outmoded and should have been dropped a long time ago. Transportation, surely, must be recognized as a primary instrument for the development of an adequate social and economic infrastructure within the provinces and regions of Canada.
That being the case, surely it is essential for there to be a significant provincial and regional input into the formulation of national transportation policy in Canada. I submit that if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport were to present to the four western premiers and, later, to the rest of the country specific proposals and ideas for a major revision of our transportation policy, they would receive in return input from these areas. An entire litany of tariffs and freight rates has been recited in this House over the years. I wanted to point out some to the Minister of Transport in detail.
In the present Parliament there have been many discussions concerning the cost of living and, particularly, the costs of food. Well, let me tell the Minister of Transport, through you, Sir, that the revenue under agreed charge rates from any part of Ontario to Vancouver with respect to a 50,000 pound carload of foodstuffs is $1.65 per ton mile. To Regina, it is $2.83 per ton mile and to Saskatoon it is even worse, $2.91 per ton mile, almost double. The freight rate is the same from all Ontario points to Vancouver as it is to Regina, $2.21 per hundredweight. For some reason, it is $2.44 per hundredweight to Saskatoon. Under the eastern rate groups, the rate from Quebec to Vancouver is $1.53 per ton mile, and $2.50 to Regina. Let me mention steel products and wire fencing. I wonder why farmers are not particularly interested in listening to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) who is in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board?

speechtext: And why they did not vote Liberal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Yes, and why did they not vote Liberal. For wire fencing, the rate from Sydney, Nova Scotia to Vancouver is $1.75 per hundredweight. To Regina it is $2.20. The revenue per ton mile is 95 cents to Vancouver, but $1,77 to Regina, almost double. To Saskatoon, it is $1.88. For angles, beams and channels as well as other steel products, the rate from Contrecoeur, Quebec, to Vancouver is $1.50 per hundredweight, but is $2.23 to Regina and $2.41 to Saskatoon.
One could recite examples of inequalities in freight rates for the whole day and not get through them all. So, here is one specific area that the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport can discuss with the premiers of the four western provinces. They can make specific proposals and come to an accommodation involving the equalization and, if necessary, subsidization of freight rates. This

should involve not only the prairie provinces, but the Maritimes as well, and should deal not only with rail freight rates, but with air transportation costs. They should be concerned not only about the movement of goods, but also about the movement of people.
It should not cost so much to fly from Halifax to Vancouver. We should be able to lower those fares and, if necessary, increase fares slightly for people travelling between Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto, the routes where traffic volume is probably 10 or 20 times greater than in other parts of the country. If we increased those fares a little, we could afford to reduce fares for people wishing to travel from Vancouver to their national capital, or from Halifax to Inuvik or anywhere else in this country. I say this because there is discrimination even in the movement of Canadians because of where they happen to live. So long as our transportation system continues to be motivated by the search for profits, we shall continue to find this kind of discrimination affecting both the movement of goods and of people. I was amazed to see a newspaper headline which read, "Lang scolds western governments". In the first place, who asked him; in the second place, who cares?
If the Prime Minister and the government are genuinely concerned about the economic problems of western Canada and, as well, their own political difficulties, they ought to realize that the big billboards the Minister of Justice erected in his riding in the last election campaign showing him whispering in the Prime Minister's ear helped them to lose most of the seats that they had held in western Canada. When are they going to realize that this man who talks about the tunnel vision of the premiers was the author of an outrageous grain stabilization bill. That did not help the Liberals in western Canada. This man was the author, and even today is the stubborn defender, of Operation Lift. Does the Prime Minister still not realize that the Minister of Justice, whom he has put in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, has contributed to western alienation and disenchantment not only with Liberals but, as well, with other matters that we have debated in western Canada for a number of years?
The Minister of Justice talks about the tunnel vision of the four western premiers. Since his vision did not extend beyond the end of his nose when he introduced Operation Lift, he is in no position to throw stones in any direction at anyone. I recall farmers, agriculturalists and members in this chamber, including some in his own party, pleading with him and warning him about the stupidity of Operation Lift. If we have one billion bushels of grain on hand, so what? That is money in the bank. That is an inventory, a pantry for the world. All it would take is an average crop in one year as well as some good sales in that year, and in 15 months we could be out of grain. I would sure like to hear the minister telling us again how good Operation Lift was.

Our transportation policy must not only take into account our geography and climate and not only have input from the provinces and regions of this country, but it must spell out the transportation requirements of the country as a whole. There must not only be equalized or subsidized freight rates, but rail passenger services must be expanded.
The federal government has a dismal record in the research and development of new, fast and modern rail transportation. Canadian National Railways and United Aircraft have been carrying the ball almost singlehanded-ly in the development of the turbo-train. They are to be congratulated on this. I hope that when it starts operating next week, it will be a magnificent success. The amount of money the government has put into the development of short take-off and landing aircraft is many times greater than any effort made in relation to ground transportation. I do not know why that kind of effort could not have been put into the development of rail transportation, trains to carry hundreds of people, not 14 or 18 as will this fancy aircraft which the minister is prone to brag about.
Our transportation policy must prohibit the abandoning of branch lines, with a few minor exceptions. The moratorium, which ends in 1975, that the government and the Canadian Transport Commission placed on the abandoning of rail lines is not good enough. The people on the prairies can foresee hundreds of miles of tracks being torn up and dozens of communities, which can and should be viable, disappearing. In spite of what the Minister of Justice said on this subject, there are too many communities in the prairie provinces of 1,000, 1,500 or 2,000 people which will be decimated by that kind of policy. That is another specific proposal which the Prime Minister can present to the four western premiers, namely that there will be no abandoning of branch lines, with only a few minor exceptions.

I challenge the Minister of Transport and the CPR to present revenue figures for all the agencies that have been closed, for example, in the Regina service centre area and compared

with that the revenue of those agencies, incoming and outgoing, carload and less than carload, when they were open agencies. I will bet the Minister of Transport a plugged nickel that that information is not available because the CPR found it very convenient not to keep track of that revenue for individual shipping points that are not open agencies. They can flatly say they were uneconomic, no longer needed and the evidence to prove otherwise has carefully been destroyed; in fact, it has not even been provided.
A new national transportation policy must provide for an integration of our transportation services, air with rail and rail with road in areas of short, medium and long haul traffic. I sometimes wonder why we need 10, 20 or 30 flights a day between Ottawa and Montreal, a distance of 120 miles, when the turbo-train or an even faster train would do the job much better between downtown Ottawa and downtown Montreal. We waste capital and make inefficient the operation of our airlines. They waste money, not only by endeavouring to transport that many people for a short distance, but trying to feed them a meal during a 50 minute flight. Surely, there is room to integrate air with ground traffic, rail or bus, on short hauls. In order to relieve congestion on our highways, there is room to integrate the moving of freight by rail on medium and long hauls and by truck on short to medium hauls.
There is a need for a co-ordination of schedules. I can recall the summer before last being on a flight from Ottawa to Winnipeg via Toronto. I arrived in Winnipeg five minutes after a flight left for Regina. I also recall the Canadian Pacific passenger train arriving in Regina 12 minutes after the CN Dayliner left for Saskatoon. This does not require legislation. All that is required is some good sense to co-ordinate our transportation companies and systems.

The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) says that would make it pay. It would be terrible if the passenger service were to pay or even reduce its losses. Government policy directives from the Minister of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission could very simply solve this situation. There is no reason why the so-called competing airlines in this country cannot have integrated schedules. The Canadian Transport Commission needs to be totally revamped, not only in terms of its members, but in terms of its authority. We must quit using it as a repository for ex-cabinet ministers and ex-railway officials. Even though they are knowledgeable and nice people, it is inconceivable that they have any real understanding or sympathy with the needs of Canadians in terms of transportation, either for their products or for themselves.
I wish to again point out that within a matter of a few days, in spite of representations by ordinary citizens, reeves, mayors of towns, the government of a province, Senators and members of parliament, the railway committee of the Canadian Transport Commission allowed the CNR to proceed with the closing of 70 agencies. All we were doing was trying to salvage even 20 of them. I submit that the CNR and CPR have yet to prove their case for the way they have been closing agencies and the validity of

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
the so-called customer service areas. The Canadian Transport Commission must be more responsive to the wishes expressed by the public, organizations and governments. If the commission is going to continue to be responsive only to the economic needs, the profit and loss statements, of railroads, airlines, steamships and interprovincial trucking companies, they will continue to be looked upon by the Canadian public as something opposed to their interests and, even more serious, opposed to the interests of this country.
We cannot continue to allow the transportation system to operate as though it were still controlled by 19th century railway barons. The lip service which successive federal governments have paid to the publicly-owned sections of our transportation system has been all too apparent year after year. Our national railway, the CNR, is still saddled with a debt it can never discharge. Almost every year the CNR shows operating profits of between $30 million and $50 million but the interest on the company's debt is $15 million to $30 million higher than that. And each year parliament votes tens of millions to pay the interest on a debt which was never the result of the operation of Canadian National. Part of a new transportation policy should be to take over as part of the national debt the remaining $2 billion owed by the CN to the banks, trust companies and some individuals, thus allowing the government, on behalf of the people, to own all the shares in the system. This would help the national railway to operate more efficiently than it has done up to now.
Another step in a constructive transportation policy would be to halt the continual erosion of Air Canada through giving rights to another airline which has never had the interests of the Canadian people at heart. The Canadian Pacific system has never at any time geared its operations to the welfare and good of the nation, but only to its own welfare. The minister has been sitting on a decision about the right to the air route to Milan for months. I bet a nickel he is going to give it to Canadian Pacific. I would be glad to lose that nickel, but I will be surprised if I am not correct. Europe was supposed to be reserved for Air Canada. But all of a sudden, Canadian Pacific got Amsterdam. Then they got Lisbon and Madrid. What do you bet, Mr. Speaker, that they are going to get Milan, too? But when the President of Air Canada suggests that Air Canada should be given much more serious consideration when it comes to rights across the Pacific, we hear a different story. Oh, no. The Canadian Pacific gets the new landing rights in China. I can only believe it is the deliberate policy of the government to prevent Air Canada from being as viable as it should be. This is being accomplished by granting lucrative rights to other companies, particularly to a corporation whose interests are not in the best interests of Canada.
My hon. friends will be dealing with other transportation issues. Most of them involve items which are not new-they are brought up time after time. If the minister wishes to put an end to some of these grievances which have been borne for decades in western Canada he should help the Prime Minister make suitable proposals to the western premiers, for one thing, and, second, he should

make sure the Minister of Justice has nothing whatever to do with the conference.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, may I say I welcome the opportunity to speak to this motion proposed by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) on behalf of his party. While acknowledging the existence of the many transportation problems to which he referred, and realizing that they are very real, it seems to me that to suggest they can all be solved simply by nationalizing all modes of transportation in the country is a gross over-simplification of the problem.
I welcome this debate because the substance of the motion is similar to that of a motion I proposed on behalf of the Conservative party in the House on March 20. At that time nothing was forthcoming by way of response from the government side. Indeed, very little of substance has been said in reply to criticism which has been advanced since that date. I have a definite suspicion, too, that there will be little of substance delivered here today, though we can, perhaps, expect more open-ended promises and assurances that these matters will be looked into.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is an able fellow, but he continues to be more effective evading questions and playing politics than he is in administering his department. I am sure he must realize that the Department of Transport is vital to the economic and social progress of the country. I shall not spend the rest of my time picking on the minister, other than to say that we on this side are extremely disappointed by the lack of policy in the area of transportation. However, we realize that the Minister of Transport is dedicated to a party which is totally bankrupt of policy in the area of transportation. It is bankrupt because it fails to acknowledge that a problem even exists. He belongs to a party which said before the election campaign that all was well in all parts of Canada, a party which failed to acknowledge that there was a transportation problem in western Canada or in the Atlantic region. How could one expect a policy in these circumstances?
We now find the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Otto) arranging to meet the western premiers in an attempt to find out what is wrong. And even before the conference can get off the ground, this lone ranger from Saskatchewan accuses the premiers of tunnel vision. I say this is another example of intellectual arrogance, the kind of arrogance which led to such a pathetic performance by his party in the last election, in western Canada. It is this same arrogance that has caused the government to fail to recognize the expertise and knowledge which some of its own supporters possessed. I refer particularly to the former member for Edmonton-Strathcona, Dr. Harries, who possessed a wealth of knowledge on the subect of transportation. On December 10, 1969, he put forward a private member's bill, Bill C-170, which zeroed in on the major issues and highlighted the points we are dealing with now. I should like to quote from this bill because it expresses so well what the debate on western transportation is all about. The substance is as follows:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this or any other Act, any person engaged for hire or reward in transport of goods or
June 19, 1973

passengers by motor vehicle or by railway to which the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada extends, who charges higher tolls or tariffs for the transport of goods or passengers for a lesser distance than for a longer distance on the same line or route, shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to pay to the shipper or passenger not less than the greater of ten thousand dollars or the difference between the actual toll or tariff charged and what the toll or tariff would have been if the lowest tariff or toll had been charged over the whole route.
Basically, this is what concerns us, the anomalies in the freight rate structure affecting western Canada which allow goods to be shipped to Vancouver for less than it would cost to ship them to Edmonton or other intermediate points in western Canada. The government disregarded this particular bill and the input that Dr. Harries was very much prepared to contribute, and thus failed to develop a policy, to overcome one of the basic issues that confront us in the West.
I am surprised that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, who has been critical of the lack of government transportation policy over the years, sees fit to keep the government in office notwithstanding the fact that this issue is so very vital and important, particularly to the future of western Canada. The only thing we can be thankful for is the message that was driven home so dramatically last October 30. We now see, superficially at least, the government acknowledging that there is a transportation problem in this country, and as a result we are going to have a western economic conference at which the subject of transportation will be the major issue.
I should like to say to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that we look forward in hopeful anticipation to something positive and satisfactory emerging from this conference in Calgary in July. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) had better go to Calgary fully armed with some positive proposals, because I do not believe that the western premiers will be satisfied with sitting down with their federal counterparts on a simple fact finding mission or exercise in public relations. Neither had these ministers better go out west simply with the idea of garnering some votes for the Liberal party, because I can assure them that these votes will be hard to find.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is not a question but an observation and I am surprised that you would allow my hon. friend to taunt me in this way. However, knowing the hon. member as I do I take it as a gesture of
Transportation Policy
good faith, and I can assure him that it is not quantity that counts over on this side but quality.
As I was saying before I was so delightfully interrupted by my hon. friend from St. Boniface, the premier of Alberta, as spokesman on transportation matters, made abundantly clear the position of the west in a speech to the Empire and Canadian Clubs in Toronto on May 7. Significantly, this speech gave rise to questions in the House to the minister regarding what positive proposals or programs the government will be putting forward at that time. I simply want to reiterate the importance of bringing forth a coherent set of proposals so that this question can be fully and exhaustively debated. The premier of Alberta had this to say:
-I want full and complete disclosure by the railroads of all the cost data that they provide the Canadian Transport Commission. I want to know the extent of fixed-as compared to variable-costs.
I want to know the economic benefit of terminals and loading facilities to major centres in Canada. I want to know the relative taxpayer contributions to other transportation facilities-such as airport terminals. In short-full disclosure by the railroads of their cost data. Second, public justification of every major freight rate in terms of cost-benefit for the Canadian public interest-not the railroads' financial interest. The railroads are common carriers. They were established historically to pull Canada together- how? Primarily by building through western Canada. In fact, to really create confederation as we know it today. Are they fulfilling their original purpose in 1973? Most westerners do not think so!
I wonder whether the Minister of Transport can answer that request in the affirmative.
We then had the speech made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) in which he said that then the provincial premiers insist on a "tunnel-vision" approach to a particular problem to try to get quick, surface answers to a problem with deep underlying causes, "we are not going to get ahead". I quote that last statement from the Vancouver Sun for June 16, 1973. With this kind of atmosphere there is going to be a conference of confrontation rather than a conference to find meaningful solutions.
I should also like to know what role the elected federal representatives are going to play at this particular conference. This group should not be totally circumvented, yet the government has been conspicuously silent on the matter. As the elected representatives of the hopes and aspirations of the people in the parliament of Canada, we have acknowledged that there are transportation and economic problems to be dealt with. Although we have spoken out on these issues our words have fallen on deaf ears. We have some knowledge of the situation and have made suggestions.
I believe it is imperative that at least a committee composed of federal members of parliament from western Canada be invited to participate at the conference, at least in the role of observers. There are eight elected members of parliament in the Liberal party from western Canada, 18 elected members of parliament in the New Democratic party and 42 elected members of parliament in the Progressive Conservative party. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, who speaks for the west in the federal parliament of Canada? Certainly, it does not appear that the Liberals do since it is obvious that they do not have the support of the west. It is equally obvious that the other two parties have a controlling majority. This is why I believe the govern-
4896

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
ment should call upon the expertise, knowledge and abilities of these elected representatives and allow them to participate at the conference, at least as observers. I ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport seriously to consider this proposal; failure to comply with this request can only be interpreted, as far as I am concerned, as an affront to western members of parliament. We known the government has never been in the habit of consulting elected representatives, but on this particular occasion-"particular" in light of the political make-up of the House-if the government fails to confide in the truly elected members of parliament representing western Canada it is simply a manifestation of its genuine lack of sincerity in grappling with problems confronting the west. Transportation is an urgent matter in western Canada and until it is solved it places an undue burden on the economy as a whole.
The motion before the house states that Canada urgently needs a new transportation policy aimed at removing regional inequalities, disparities and so forth. I agree with that statement, Mr. Speaker. But I believe that a national transportation policy must go beyond that. We must develop an effective national transportation policy within the framework of our industrial goals. I believe we must adopt an over-all, co-ordinated approach, and by so doing provide greater opportunities in all regions and promote and preserve national unity. Our transportation policy must apply not only to rail transportation but to all other modes, such as air, marine and surface transportation. I believe our national transportation policy must be utilized as a major tool for economic development in all regions of Canada. Such a policy cannot be developed by the carriers alone. It must be developed by the federal government, it must be supported and it must be effectively administered and co-ordinated by the federal government. A national transportation policy must be embodied in an over-all national policy with goals and objectives that would enhance the development and preservation of the economic and social welfare of all Canadians, regardless of where they live.
Over the past few years, as a result of the government's attempt to overcome regional economic disparities, we have witnessed huge outlays of money under the DREE program. The net effect I believe has been minimized, indeed swallowed, by discriminatory freight rates. In some cases very high freight rates apply to industries locating in some of these depressed areas in respect of the movement of their goods to the marketplace, and I refer here particularly to the western and Atlantic areas. I suggest a rechannelling of funds might be more effective to the development of a national transport network. Perhaps this would have a more stimulating effect on industry in those regionally depressed areas, as they would at least have the advantage of seeing their product move to the marketplace at realistic rates. This would probably also alleviate the risk of the imposition of countervailing measures by some of the countries to which we move our goods.
In short, I believe a re-evaluation of the DREE program should be undertaken to compare the effect those funds would provide if used to improve the transportation network. If this were done we would certainly overcome,

perhaps once and for all, some of the anomalies that exist from one end of the country to the other, and certainly alleviate the pressures in respect of national unity.
It has been said in this House many times, said in the press and said by speakers of all political affiliations that in this country there are inequities, discrepancies and anomalies in the freight rate structure, some of which have been devastatingly discriminatory. I will not go into them in detail because, as I have said before, they are widely known. Just to mention a few, we might consider the movement of goods from east to west at one rate and the movement the other way at a totally different rate. We might consider the differential in the rate on the movement of processed goods from west to east, which is twice the rate on raw products moving the same direction. We see greater charges for shorter distances than for longer distances, a point alluded to by our friend Dr. Harries in his Bill C-170. We also see the absence of freight rate groupings in western Canada, and I could go on.
These issues have been around for many years. They have been the subject of controversial discussion, commissions, studies and hearings, yet we are still entrenched with the underlying philosophy that we in the west are only good for supplying raw materials. To put the matter into perspective, we must look at the current legislation now governing-

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I thank hon. members for allowing me the privilege to continue. I shall do so briefly. I thought we were allotted a little more time. I simply want to say that under the provisions of the National Transportation Act there are three safeguards in respect of which I now cannot go into detail. They have not proved effective in protecting the interests of the shipper. Therefore, I think this whole concept of the Canadian Transport Commission, its role and structure, has to be reviewed and reoriented.
The absence of any effective legislation has created inequities and unfairness in the establishment of freight rates. In terms of dollars and cents, the discriminatory features and the application of our freight rates in the west has cost us something in the order of $20 million annually. We have inter-regional trade deficits of something in the order of $2 billion annually. The loss of jobs as a result of our inability to establish industry in western Canada runs into the thousands.
I simply want to reiterate the very urgent and pressing necessity of coming up with an effective transportation policy which will take into consideration the economic development aspects of all regions in Canada, and reiterate once again that our transportation policy must become a tool for economic development. The structure and role of the Canadian Transportation Commission must be examined and reoriented with that in mind. The public must have greater participation in decisions affecting transportation in this country. If competition is to be a factor in rate-setting devices, Part III of the National Transporta-
June 19, 1973

tion Act must not only be proclaimed, it must be implemented.
We must have a complete and thorough review of freight rate structures as they apply to all regions of Canada. We must examine the principle and the application of agreed charges and non-competitive commodity rates to eliminate the regional discrimination which arises therefrom. We must establish a mechanism that will provide some unity and fairness of rates across the country, based upon the distance travelled. We must remove the anomolies in respect of the cost of moving goods between regions. We must upgrade our rail lines and our roadbeds if we are to haul heavier loads.
We must also consider in very short order major improvements to the ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert. We must broaden the use of these facilities in order to achieve maximum benefit for the agricultural producers of western Canada.
In respect of rail line abandonment, we must realize that rail service is an important and essential aspect of the welfare and preservation of our rural lifestyle. Further, rural rail line abandonment decisions must take into consideration the over-all social effects upon communities as well as economic factors. We must consider amending the criteria of abandonment and discontinuance procedures for lines operating on a non-profit basis. We must also devise a subsidy structure, where necessary, to encourage economic and efficient service, and we must thoroughly and immediately review any abandonment decisions and procedures, considering carefully the impact upon communities and the people affected.
I realize I have abused my privilege, Mr. Speaker, but I simply want to close with this point. It is my belief that in a complex society and economy such as ours, transportation is a major factor, and certainly a significant link in uniting the west and Atlantic provinces with the mainstream of confederation. There are other factors to consider as well, such as capital, technology, people and environment, but none so important now as transportation. Without a sensible and satisfactory transportation policy, the job of broadening the economic base, and thereby the opportunities which arise, would be a formidable task. I want to urge this government to get on with the job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House now has before it a motion of special importance as it raises crucial and vital problems concerning our country's economy, in which we can see shocking regional disparities and social inequalities from coast to coast.
The motion reads as follows:
That this House is of the opinion that Canada urgently needs a new national transportation policy, aimed at removing regional inequalities and disparities, and including amongst other things the equalizing of the freight rate structure, the discontinuance of the practice of abandoning railway lines and services, and the greater use of the Ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert.
Mr. Speaker, as one can see this motion is acceptable as it stands since special problems are raised and since the government is being asked to table in this House a truly national transportation policy, a just policy, particularly
Transportation Policy
as regards tariffs, in order to ensure fair and equal treatment in every part of the country.
In the course of my brief remarks, Mr. Speaker, that will certainly lead me to speak of the difference in the cost price of feed grain between eastern and western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, everyone will agree with me that, because of the immensity of our country, if we are to ensure constant progress for our society, we require a national transportation policy that takes account of the country's size. There is no need for me to elaborate on this. I need only remind you of the debates which occurred at the time of confederation, when people dreamed of a railway that would unite Canada. This was one of the sine qua non conditions for the preservation of the country's unity, the unity of the Canadian confederation. Now we see what the result has been.
One special aim of a transportation policy is to minimize communication difficulties. In this respect, private enterprise plays an important part. There are new companies, such as Telesat, for example, a semi-public Crown corporation which is trying to participate, but a great deal of work remains to be done since many regions still lack communications media, which is unacceptable.
For instance, with regard to television, I am thinking of New Brunswick and other areas of Canada.
There is another objective we must pursue, we must not neglect, which goes beyond political aspirations, and that is ensuring equal opportunities to all Canadians, wherever they live.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to feed grains transport policy, we have one law for our friends and another for our foes, and that no one can deny. Eastern producers have to pay almost one dollar more per bushel than their counterparts elsewhere in Canada. There is also a difference between British Columbia and the western provinces, again because of that tariff policy.
Mr. Speaker, that policy is a source of discontent, it divides Canadians; as a result of it, the present national transport policy does not pursue the objective it should have, that of guaranteeing equal opportunities to all Canadians wherever they may be.
Every producer, whether from eastern or from western Canada, whatever he is growing, should have the same requirements, the same responsability and the same rights with respect to commissions, be the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Feed Board or any other commission. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, we contribute to divide the country.
Last week in Drummondville, about 10 Liberal members and one minister-Creditist members were also well represented-took part in a dialogue with spokesmen for the Farm Producers Union which, along with the Milk Producers Federation and other organizations as well as co-operatives and four-mills, represents the "speaking majority" in Quebec as regards that problem. And what did we hear all through the evening? Those people were disatisfied, and rightly so, and not one of the members who were there can say the opposite. Those people were calling for a just treatment; they wanted to have a voice in the Canadian Wheat Board, in the Canadian Feed Board and, since the evil can be traced back to it, they especially
26446-20J

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
called for an equitable transport policy that would enable eastern producers to benefit from western production and western producers to have access to Quebec manufactured products.
Mr. Speaker, of course the hon. members there could not help agreeing to the requests of those people and admitting they were right, since that is the price of national unity, of building this country on sound bases.
Mr. Speaker, there is another aspect I should like to mention. In 1969, the Canadian National Railways made a request covering a large part of the province of Quebec in order to establish the station-center system and to close local stations, to replace station masters by some robot who earns from $25 to $40 a month and can only give parcels, and open or close doors, and to set a Zenith phone system so that the public could have access to information or make reservations.
Mr. Speaker, in 1969 the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will recall-he was a member of parliament then but was not in charge of that department-that the House passed Bill C-7 to grant an increase in subsidies to Canadian National Railways. At the same time, the CNR submitted a formal request to close those stations and abandon complete lines.
Mr. Speaker, I will quote names of companies to show the impact that situation has created. In Fortierville, for example, in the constituency of Lotbiniere, there is a flour mill; Deschaillons is the home of Montreal Terra Cotta Limited, Commercial Office Furniture, Potvin and Fournier, etc. In Parisville, another small town, there is the Henri Cote co-operative enterprise and many more. The Vital Boucher and Les Machineries agricoles companies are located in Leclercville. All these companies were working towards the same goal as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, namely the creation of jobs and the maintenance of steady expansion in this region of the country.
Mr. Speaker, all these companies were supplied by means of the railway that passed through there, the famous Parisville line. Then Canadian National Railways petitioned to be allowed to abandon precisely that line. On the one hand you have a department investing money by the millions to create jobs-which is wonderful-and on the other hand you have a Crown corporation, Canadian National, trying to do away with the usual means of transport.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that these two programs are contradictory. In spite of the entreaties of the authorities of all the municipalities, in spite of the protests of the owners of the small Quebec enterprises involved, Canadian National Railways turned a deaf ear and the railway line was abandoned.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-7, adopted in late November or early December 1969, granted more than $400 million in grants of all kinds to finance the national railroads. Before this act was passed, the railway companies received for transportation, in 1967 for example, $110 million a year in federal grants to compensate them for fares and services operated at a loss.

I know that the Minister of Transport will answer back because he is one of those who say: "We must abandon the services which are unprofitable." I am one of those who say: "The first role of the government is to make transportation available in order to unite the country, even at a loss." Anyway, this Parliament and this government, as the previous ones, have constantly voted millions of dollars to make up for losses incurred by the CNR.
Under the 1967 legislation, those grants were supposed to decrease gradually by $14 million a year beginning in 1968 and be completely removed by 1975. As a result, following the process provided in the legislation, the railway companies had until 1975 to ask permission to abolish all unprofitable services and branch lines while continuing to get subsidies for services which must be maintained in the public interest.
Now, who defines public interest, Mr. Speaker? One would have to go to the Canadian Transport Commission to find out, and there should be someone who speaks French there. No additional financing would be granted through this bill, unless the total amount does not exceed the decreasing amount from year to year, if it were possible. Therefore, that was the situation in which the Canadian National Railways found themselves in 1969. They ask for additional financing on one hand and, on the other hand, for leave to abandon services which supposedly run at a deficit.
Mr. Speaker, this House is now considering a bill which will probably be passed before adjournment, Bill C-164, and when reading it we can find that the Canadian National Railways are asking us again more than $225 million, and authority to borrow an additional amount to pay for deficits of previous years.
It is interesting to note, if one wants to be earnest, that when they want to stop providing services on some lines, the CN authorities spare no efforts to keep very tight accounts and prove that these services are not profitable. We only have to refer to all the reports that the Canadian National Railways presented with their request to justify their application to stop providing services. But when they want to establish a new concept such as the central station plan, these very officials say that profits are secondary and that modernizing services must come first.
This is probably what the minister will tell us as well. In short, the economic argument is used whenever convenient. However, this is taxpayers' money and they are entitled to know how it is used.
In the current situation the lines which served the farmers are abandoned while, on the other hand, subsidies are requested and a bushel of wheat is more costly to an eastern producer than to any other producer in Canada. This is completely unacceptable.
This is why I support the motion presented by the New Democratic party which is aimed at inciting the government to develop a new and truly national transport policy which would take into account the vastness of our country.
In a brief which I submitted to the Canadian Transport Commission on December 16, 1969, I stated and I quote:
The supporters of the Canadian National Railways policy will maintain that it is impossible for the railway companies not to
June 19, 1973

show a deficit if they are not relieved from their obligations to sustain deficit services. Consequently-
-as current transport authorities do,-
-they maintain it is in the INTEREST OF CANADIANS who are paying taxes . . . and who are therefore subsidizing the railway companies not to pay unnecessarily for services which will always be non profitable.
And they go even farther today. While having taxpayers swallow that, primary and important railway lines are abandoned.
On the other hand, you have the status quo policy supporters. They maintain-
-perhaps for political reasons-
-that nothing should be changed in the current policy. However the current policy,-
Mr. Speaker, this policy spells deficits which we have to finance and about which western and eastern Canadians are dissatisfied anyway. Just listen to the speeches made in the House by the hon. members and you will realize this.
Finally, there are the supporters of a policy of the future for the National Railways. They demand better services, a realignment of costs, an adjustment of the National Railways to the needs of Canada's modern society. Personally, I should willingly include myself in this third category-
-with my colleagues,-
-and a great number of-
-our fellow citizens from the province of Quebec.
Apparently, the National Railways have fallen behind the situation. Therefore, our propositions are certainly not extremist.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the present situation cannot go on any longer. Many CNR services would greatly need to be improved, rechecked in order to best serve the economic interests of the underdeveloped regions and thus remove regional disparities, a task which the minister wants so much to be done.
Besides, in that spirit, the federal government has set up-
-we will recall that the Minister of Transport was then at the head of that department -a Regional Economic Expansion Department-
And, Mr. Speaker, should he be recognized later, I would like it if the minister could tell the House if his department was consulted by the Canadian Transport Commission and by the CNR before the abandonment of some railway lines at the time he himself was working out his new policy.
Mr. Speaker, now that I have touched on the points I wanted to emphasize, I would like to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the motion be amended by substituting a comma for the period and by adding the following:
"and that this new national transportation policy make special allowance for the differences in the cost price of feed grains between eastern and western Canada so as to ensure a fair price for all Canadian agricultural producers."
-wherever they live.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the opposition was well advised when it decided to devote its time today to the very important problem of transport in Canada. That is just about the only point on which I agree with hon. members who have spoken so far. As for the other points, I intend to deal with them separately.
To my mind, we say things that are obvious when we speak of the size of this country, of the inacessibility of certains areas, of the remoteness of certain communities, and of the fact that ensuring an equally efficient service to all is possible only to the extent where we endow ourselves with a transport system capable of enabling the people not only to visit each other, not only to travel across the country, but also to transport freight, and of allowing all Canadians to benefit from Canada to a greater extent.
Now, the problem is important to Canada, as it would be to any other country, but more so for Canada because it is sparsely populated; let us not forget that in the United States, where the population exceeds 220 million, building a railroad from New York to Los Angeles would cost no more than building one from Halifax to Vancouver, but for one difference: there are 220 million people to pay for it over there, against our 20 million here. That is a reality we cannot deny or shut our eyes to.
The problem of transports in Canada must therefore be studied from every angle. It is complex, extremely expensive for the people of Canada, and I too would like it to be defined.
I read the resolution of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) which deals with a national policy. That is the very purpose of the resolution; it asks the government to come up with a national transport policy. Hon. members have spoken of everything, except that. Grievances were brought up, such as that dealing

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
with the difference in freight rates between western cities and Vancouver; feed grains were mentioned, but no one dared define a national transport policy.
There is one good reason, Mr. Speaker, that is a national transport policy in Canada could exist only if it is related to regional programs-because each region has particular problems and geography. Some of those areas can be reached only by waterways, others by railways and there is the problem of remote areas. Then, as far as the national transport policy in Canada is concerned, we must talk about regional programs, because the transport issue in western Canada is not the same as the one in the Mari-times; there is a big difference. And we must absolutely consider specific solutions for each region.
Now, what does transport mean? First, it is a service not an industry, even though we can call it an industry with a specific sense. It is a kind of service and we must elaborate our transport policy in order to reach our economic social and national objectives, that is to elaborate our various transport systems in relation to objectives and purposes that we are trying to reach as a national entity.
People do travel, Mr. Speaker. They travel in their community, their region, from one region to the other, throughout the country and abroad. They travel by ship, by aircraft, by train, on the highway; so, all sorts of problems crop up.
Now, the federal government has a wide jurisdiction in the field of transportation; the provinces also have a certain jurisdiction and we must find for every region a policy truly appropriate to its requirements and acceptable to all Canadians because they must be prepared to pay for it.
I heard the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) state that we must not disturb anything in the existing services. After saying that we must review and change everything, he adds in the same breath that we must preserve the status quo, that we must maintain the services.
Obviously, everybody will agree that if it takes 100 miles of tracks to serve a farm somewhere-perhaps I exaggerate-it would probably be better to close it down.
Anyway, that problem does not exist now since all those branch lines have been frozen some years ago; no railroad lines have been abandoned and until 1975, I think, nobody will have to suffer from that in Canada. Obviously, we will probably have the opportunity to discuss what will happen after that.
We are being told about a national railroad and transportation policy and I am not expecting hon. members sitting on the other side of the House to think that the government has done something; it is sure that theoretically and as a rule, it is necessary for it to do nothing. And that is done with much intelligence by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who spends his time distorting everybody's words because it amuses him. Anyway, if Canada were represented only by this

kind of persons, I think we would have a very poor Parliament.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, contrarily to what is being said, I have been trying for some time to work with the provinces. A while back someone said that the provinces should be called upon to contribute. That is of course what I have done. The first meeting which I had was with the premiers of the Maritimes to whom I presented concrete proposals, in order to solve certain problems. No one mentioned the fact that grants are being given in the Maritimes, that 30 per cent of the grants are in the field of railway transportation and not only in this area, but also in the trucking field because today we cannot simply give grants to the railways since there is trucking transportation which is becoming more and more important, even in western Canada.
I had figures before my eyes a moment ago and I realize that half the trucks in Canada are in western Canada; in fact, of the 1,500,000 trucks in Canada, 800,000 are in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. In other words, this transportation means is extremely important and we must see how we can use it to reach our national objectives. Now, I have met with the Maritimes premiers; we have talked about freight rates, we have arrived at sound propositions. I have also talked about coasting, that is about the Darling report, in an attempt to see if the premiers would consider positively the repatriation of our ships in order that the coastal transportation could be assured by Canadian ships and crews. We have discussed at length and I am expecting answers to questions that have been raised. I hope that we will soon arrive at a new agreement.
Thus, those who believe that we are not working in conjunction with the provinces are wrong. I asked all the ministers of transport to meet with me in Manitoba, in Brandon I believe, and they thought it preferable to attend the big western opportunities conference before meeting the Minister of Transport. That was their strategy. I do not believe it was a delaying tactic, but simply that they wanted to get a general view of the problem. Thus I was prepared to work with them, and I am still prepared to do so. We did the same thing with British Columbia, Mr. Speaker. We studied the entire transportation system in the north of the province; we also studied the effect of the use of the harbours, particularly in Prince Rupert, and the hon. member for Saint-Boniface (Mr. Guay) will undoubtedly have the opportunity to speak about that. We worked and negotiated for months, and today we are very close to an agreement, since the leaks are starting. But this time they are coming not from the federal government, but from that of British Columbia.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, all I am saying is that when one has made such progress, one can disagree with what the department is doing, but I believe that broad general statements that nothing is being done about the railways, that the problem of feed grains is being overlooked, are without foundation. The hon. member for Lotbiniere would be astounded at the number of hours of work we have devoted to finding a solution to this problem and, I have no doubt, it will very soon be solved. That then is-
June 19, 1973

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Not at all, Mr. Speaker. There are all those problems. There is the problem of the various rates pointed out by a member for Calgary, for example, between some western cities and Vancouver and from Vancouver to eastern areas. It is clear that if it costs $2.50 to ship goods to Winnipeg and it only costs $1.50 to send them to Vancouver, it is difficult to explain. I would be rather reluctant to appear before a meeting of westerners to explain such an inconsistent matter which the railways can however explain, there is no doubt about it, because they find an explanation. If the member for Winnipeg would stop playing his discordant tune, it would enable me to complete my remarks.
Anyhow, Mr. Speaker, it is surely difficult. The railway companies explain it quite simply; they consider that they are competing with the maritime transport from Montreal or Halifax, through the Panama canal up to Vancouver. Those companies base their policy on the following reasoning; We absolutely have to compete with the maritime tariff. This is how they explain the situation.
But, I still believe that that argument can never be accepted by the Canadian public because it is a matter that represents, at first sight, an extremely hateful feature, and I intend to discuss the matter with the companies involved in order to remove these anomalies in relation to rates and then to be able to consider the real problems so that we will stop bringing back all transport problems in Canada to anomalies that can be explained historically, but have little reason to be maintained in 1973.
Then, we are told that we are doing nothing in the modern transport area. Mr. Speaker, why say that? As a matter of fact, a great many things are being done. We have the Turbo train that will be put in operation soon. It had a sad experience at the beginning, no doubt, but if we think of all those who devoted themselves to research in this area, they have had some sad experiences of their own, Mr. Speaker. The CNR has had its share with this train. There is the whole development being conducted on the light trains called the LRC-Light and Rapid Car. This is properly a Canadian enterprise that will be very useful.
Transportation Policy
Now, when people compare this type of transportation with the STOL program, of course they are talking about two different things. STOL aircraft, whether the Twin Otter of the THC-7, will certainly serve other purposes than the trains. There are places where small aircraft are more practical than trains travelling 250 miles an hour. Therefore, we must try to organize all this in order to better serve our people.
Consultations have taken place with the Atlantic provinces, the western provinces, British Columbia and, now, I hope that this conference scheduled for late July, again with the western provinces, will give concrete results and settle several of the problems which have been mentioned this afternoon and which certainly do exist.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
What did the hon. member say, Sir? All right.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the problem concerning airports. We did not talk much about it this afternoon as it is a highly politicized issue and each time we want to establish an airport, it stirs up protest and some members, instead of trying to overcome their political partisanship, instead of trying to make some people understand that it is in the interest of the area to build those airports, prefer to barter with their feelings. This may bring them a few votes, but I do not think it serves the interests of the country as a whole.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, in the past it was a blessing when this happened. That is to say that in several areas in Canada getting an airport was a blessing whereas in some others it was a curse. However, I think the government should be strong enough to put up with a certain unpopularity so that a few years from now the larger Canadian centres will not be poorly served by a transportation system which is obviously essential in this country; indeed jets have probably played a greater part in Canadian unity by allowing people to travel, to meet, to get acquainted and also, in most cases-and I hope it will become increasingly true-to appreciate each other highly.
We have established a policy concerning airports; we did not talk much about it, but we have one. Why, for instance, do we intend to build a new runway in Vancouver? It is not to annoy the people there, but rather because Vancouver is the gateway to Canada for the whole Far East and it is absolutely essential that this city be able to serve efficiently its people and all its visitors as well.
Now, let us speak about cargo. Today, cargo is transported not only by rail or by ship, but also by plane.
General statements are made; of course, I shall never vote for this motion. If I had been a member of the New Democratic Party, I would have fought to keep one of my colleagues from introducing a motion which, on the whole, risks destroying the little bit of economic unity which may remain in this country. Mr. Speaker, it states, and I quote: -the equalizing of the freight rate structure-
If they achieve this, the West as well as the Maritimes will be the first victims. This means that Ontario, which is

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
highly industrialized, and Montreal, will be able to compete with the few industries existing out west and in the Maritimes. So, what is this policy? What do they want to do? These are big words: Let us equalize the freight rate structure in Canada. To equalize it would mean that the poor provinces would become poorer and would be unable to get out of their fix. Furthermore, it is basically wrong to have the people believe that all existing regional problems are related to transportation.
I say one thing, Mr. Speaker: even if it cost nothing to transport certain products, industries would not set up in certain areas of the country to manufacture them. It is not true that transportation is invariably and systematically a factor of industrial localization. Such is not the case. So they retort: There exist transportation problems, and if the freight issue is solved, prosperity will come to the maritime provinces or the west. Unfortunately, that is not true. That does not mean that nothing can be done about it.
In the Maritime provinces we have been asked to increase our grants; we are going to do something and we will do it on a selective basis; in other words, industries which do not really need them will not receive any, because that becomes an injustice also. If we subsidize transport for one industry in the Maritimes which competes with another industry in Ontario, and neither of the two is at a disadvantage compared with the other as regards transport, by what right should be subsidize one? By what right should be take public funds to create such a situation? This means that we should endeavour to find areas which are in need, the sectors which can expand within slower growth areas, and give them a hand by setting reasonable rates.
It is said that we have done nothing in the area of transportation. Yet in recent years Canada has spent more than $1 billion for highways, an area which is normally under provincial jurisdiction. In fact, the Trans-Canada Highway alone cost more than $800 million to the country, precisely to join the different regions. Now, we conclude special agreements. The hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), a former premier of Nova Scotia, knows that we negotiate special agreements under the old Atlantic Development Board. Considerable amounts have been spent to give the Maritime provinces an appropriate road network. Since then, we have continued along these lines through the FRED agreements with each province, so much so that these last years we have been spending in the Maritime provinces almost $300 million over and above the money allocated for their stretch of the Trans-Canada Highway.
Thus, it is not true to say that nothing has been done in Canada in the area of transportation. It is one of the serious problems in Canada. It involves tremendous outlays but a considerable effort is being made. Of course the problems of development in the north of British Columbia are not the same as in the Eastern Townships. Agreements are made between the two railways, the British Columbia Railway and the Canadian National, in order to try to develop natural resources of the north of British Columbia. For the province, that is more important now than to enjoy the service of a crack train between two points.

We should not forget that transportation is changing rapidly. People used to think-and they still do in some circles-that the more we build big planes, the greater the pollution and that it will be necessary to have longer and longer runways. Not so. Actually, the most recent aircraft like the DC-10 or the Lockheed 1011 require shorter runways than DC-8 type aircraft, make less noise and, eventually, will produce less pollution.
Then, we must change a little our concepts and that is why it is so important to develop the STOL program which will enable some communities to be linked together, and which can bring about, at the same time, a substantial industrial growth in this country.
This is why we are trying to introduce innovations in this field. Some people suggest that we have not the least improved in the area of air transportation. But it is not so. As a matter of fact, we have had talks with Germany in order to extend Canadian airline routes. We have discussed with Italy, China and this is why, if the hon. member wants to know, we have assigned the China route to CP Air. And now we are developing a general policy which we hope will establish for quite some time limits within which each of our two carriers will have to expand.
And I hardly think I should stand for lectures on the way we should treat Air Canada, which has never been so badly treated as by an individual whose name is Doug Fisher, whom the hon. member from a riding in Calgary knows quite well. This reporter wrote the most revolting article about Air Canada, and about the so-called French combine within the Department of Transport, which would have attempted to undermine Air Canada to the advantage of other companies. Well, we are perfectly aware that that person is able to have control over 16 members of parliament who have expressed their opinion in this House. I suggest that this is discrimination and that it does much more harm to Air Canada than anything else.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, we must develop our maritime policy, that we have stated. We try to have the biggest possible merchant fleet in Canada and to make it economically viable. We already have some elements of it on the Great Lakes; if we can have the Darling report approved, this would mean that coastal transportation will be done by Canadian ships and crews. If we can reserve the whole navigation of the Great North to Canadian crews and ships, we shall do it. And this will be extremely important, not only for transportation purposes, but for the prosperity of our shipyards across Canada.
It must not be said that we have not established a policy; we have. Rather they are programs that mesh together and are strongly regionalized. It cannot be otherwise, Mr. Speaker, because instead of serving the country well we would serve it badly.
Mr. Speaker, our transportation system in Canada is based on two principles: first, the principle of competition between various means of transportation and, then, an organization which is called the Canadian Transport Commission and which is empowered to regulate. Why has the CTC been established? In order to prevent public exploitation in regions where there is no competition. Where there is competition, the principle of the 1967 law applies and competition must determine the prices. I did not draft that

law on my own; it was adopted by the House and I cannot recall that our friends from the opposition rose against this basic principle which is part and parcel of the law. Thus, the CTC enacts regulations when there is no competition and where competition exists, the regular rivalry prevails between transportation means.
Now where grants are provided, as in the maritime provinces and eastern Quebec, we have to do as much for the trucking industry-and rightly so.
As to the changes to be made, we should know what it will cost the Canadian people. I do not mind; people may say: It does not cost anything to travel across Canada. However, we know that it is going to cost something; taxes will have to be imposed so that a company unable to remain self-sufficient with its rates may keep operating.
As a whole, Mr. Speaker, we certainly have not solved everything and we certainly will not solve everything. I hope that at the coming conference of the western premiers, we shall remove those irritants that were explained in this House. I hope they will find an interesting system for the transportation of feed grain and that the next time a day is devoted to the transportation problem, we shall really deal with a transportation policy, with its importance, because people do not always react the way we would like, since they are free.
Some people may say: Let us use trains rather than automobiles. Everybody will agree. However, it always concerns somebody else, not themselves. They drive their car, and trains are not used or rapidly become non profitable. That is true.
On the other hand, other people will say; Instead of travelling by air between Montreal and Ottawa, why not go by train? Under what principle would the government prevent any one from flying to Montreal if that is what he wants? It is clear. If ever we establish a rapid transportation system between urban centres like Ottawa and Montreal featuring crack trains as I saw in Munich, Germany, at Krauss-Maffei's that will be some improvement. This means that it is possible that within a few years trains will be travelling safely at 200 or 250 miles an hour. If this is possible our transport philosophy will be completely modified because surely people will more willingly travel by train than crowd our airports.
In Munich I have been able to see the problems caused by airports and modern transport. It took me less than six hours to fly from Montreal to Paris and one hour and a half from the Paris Airport to Paris because the highway was so bottled-up.
We also are faced with this kind of problem in the Metro-Toronto area. Extremely serious transportation problems exist and we try to solve them in co-operation with the provincial government. It is another example where we co-operate with the provincial government to solve this problem which is prevailing in our main urban centers. What can I do about it? Everybody cannot live in Toronto! We must find high-speed transportation means.
Besides we want to do the same thing in Vancouver with the co-operation of the British Columbia government.
From the main critics I have heard until now I recall abnormalities in the freight transportation rates and we agree that we should try to eliminate them. Some regions
Transporta tion Policy
are more underprivileged than others; we are going to correct that in co-operation with the provinces, with the people faced with the transportation problems so that it becomes easy to live in this country precisely because travelling distances will have been reduced through the implementation of rational transportation both for people and for goods.
