speechtext:
He can't take it, so he leaves the House. But the fact that at the conference to be held between the four western premiers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) next month one of the main items on the agenda will be the whole question of transportation and transportation costs is surely evidence that the people of western Canada, regardless of party, are vitally concerned and upset about what they consider to be the unfair way in which transportation policies presently operate to the

detriment of the people who live in the four prairie provinces. An efficient transportation system at fair rates is essential if the have-not parts of Canada, which include not only the prairie region but northern Ontario, northern Quebec and the Maritimes, are to be able to use the full potential of the natural products they possess and of the manpower available to them. If the areas I have mentioned have been unable to use their full potential, if their unemployment rates are far higher than the national average, it is to a large extent because the transportation policies pursued in this country have failed to meet the needs of those areas.
The geography of western Canada, part of which I represent, places restraints on the Prairies which are unfair to that region and which a.e not felt by other regions of the country. These restraints can only be overcome through the development of a national transportation policy which actively promotes the development of the have-not areas. I say that the prairie provinces are tired of simply being producers of raw materials, producers of wheat, poultry, paper,potash, oil and natural gas. The prairie provinces want to develop secondary industry so as to give to those who were born and who grew up in those areas the same opportunity to find jobs at good wages as is now available to people in the Toronto-Hamilton area or in the metropolitan area of Montreal. They are tired of seeing the transportation system of this country focused in such a way as to bring new jobs to areas which already have the most jobs. They want a transportation system and regulations which will permit optimum industrial and resource development in western Canada and in the Maritimes.
The philosophy presently embodied in the National Transportation Act relies almost exclusively on carrier competition to control transportation costs. This policy works to the detriment of economic development in the west. It should be co-ordinated with regional development strategy to ensure equality of opportunity. I am glad to hear that the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) intends to speak in this debate. I know he has lots of nerve. Indeed, some people would say he has lots of gall.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Not only nerve, but common sense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I want to hear him defend the present policy. Let us see who has the common sense. Hundreds of millions of dollars were paid out by people in all parts of Canada for the development of the St. Lawrence Seaway. I think this was a good move. The opening of the Seaway led to a reduction in freight rates, mainly to Quebec and Ontario. It permitted grain ships to move all the way to Thunder Bay; it permitted ore to be carried to Hamilton without having to be trans-shipped into smaller vessels. As I say, rates in Ontario and Quebec were brought down, to a large extent because of the millions which were invested in the Seaway by the people of Canada.
Manitoba, which I, and the hon. member for St. Boniface happen to represent, has a port, the Port of Churchill. It could do far more than serve the province of Manitoba. It is, in fact, a gateway to Europe for all the prairie provinces. Support for the development of the port of Churchill is given by all people of western Canada, regardless
June 19, 1973

of political affiliation. There is no harsher critic of present federal government policies, including policies of transportation, than the present leader of the Liberal party in Manitoba. He has talked more like a separatist than any other politician in the past 25 years. The Minister ot Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) can shake his head, but the record is there. His statements have been reported very extensively in the Winnipeg Free Press, so the minister can check what I say to see whether it is correct.
Let us look at what is happening at Churchill. First of all, with its inadequate facilities the port is not being used to capacity, despite the fact that the rate of shipping grain from Churchill to Europe is substantially less than the rate for shipping grain to Europe via the Great Lakes. The minister says he wants some facts, not theories, so let me give him some examples. Grain shipped from Canada via the port of Churchill to Belgium, Holland and Germany costs $4.58 per long ton; shipped via the Great Lakes it costs $8.28 per long ton. Grain shipped from Canada via Churchill to the United Kingdom costs $7.43 per long ton; via the Great Lakes it costs $10.45 per long ton, a difference of $3.02 per long ton, or almost 50 per cent more than the cost via Churchill. In spite of this, what do we have in terms of helping to develop Churchill from the federal government, from the Department of Transport, from the CNR, from the Wheat Board? Nothing at all.
Let us compare some other rates on goods shipped from Churchill. Electrical machinery shipped to Winnipeg via Churchill costs $64; via Montreal it will cost $80.20. The distance from Churchill to Winnipeg is 978 miles; the distance from Montreal to Winnipeg is 1,354 miles, almost half the distance again. Yet the two rates are almost comparable. The cost of shipping steel sheets and plates from Churchill to Winnipeg, a distance of 978 miles, is $57.60; from Montreal, a distance of 1,354 miles, the cost is less, $52.80. If you applied the Montreal rate to shipments to Winnipeg from Churchill, the rate would be $38.14 instead of the present $57.60. In other words, the rate would be $19.46 cheaper, and it means that the Montreal rate should be $14.66 less than the present rate from Montreal.
Let us examine the shipping rates on automobiles to Regina. The cost of shipping an automobile weighing 2,000 pounds from Churchill to Regina, a distance of 844 miles, is $126. The cost of shipping the same automobile from Montreal to Regina, a distance of 1,711 miles and almost twice as far, is $82.20. I hope that the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) is listening, because I should like him to explain these discrepancies and to tell the people of western Canada how these rates can be considered in any way fair. It costs $43.80 more to ship a 2,000 pound car from Churchill to Regina than it does from Montreal, even though the distance from Churchill to Regina is 867 miles less.
The minister has asked for some concrete illustrations of what should be done in terms of explaining and defending this motion. First of all, I suggest to the minister that the port facilities in Churchill can and should be improved. I suggest to the minister that if icebreakers can be used to keep the port facilities of Montreal open for
Transportation Policy
most of the year, icebreakers can equally be used to extend the season at Churchill for another two months. I suggest to the minister that if, as the premiers of western Canada have argued for years, insurance rates on cargo shipped through Churchill are too high, the government of Canada should co-operate with the provinces and set up a government insurance plan which would reduce the rates of insurance on shipments through Churchill. These are things which can be done for the port of Churchill.
Western Canada suffers because, as I said earlier, there is no real competition in the west in the transportation field. The situation has been aggravated because the railway companies, both the CPR and the CNR, began some years ago buying up trucking companies which used to be the only competitors to the railway companies. It was bad enough that they bought up the trucking companies, but to a very large extent, having bought them up, they closed them down. This was done by arranging that goods formerly shipped by truck should now be sent piggy-back on the railways. I do not question that many products can be sent piggy-back on the railways more cheaply than shipping them via trucking companies. But what happens when individual trucking companies which used to compete with the railways are bought out and driven out of business? We in western Canada know what happens because we are used to it. When there is no more competition both the CNR and the CPR really stick western Canadians, because there is no other way for western Canadian consumers or producers to ship their commodities.
Similarly, the way in which the railways set up rates as between long and short haul freight shipments completely discriminates against western Canada, and I am assuming against the maritime provinces too, though as a western member I have more information about the situation in western Canada. Let me give the House a couple of illustrations, Mr. Speaker. To ship iron and steel products from Toronto to Vancouver you pay $1.68 per 100 pounds. To ship the same 100 pounds of iron and steel products from Toronto to Saskatoon, which according to my geography is just about half the distance, you pay not $1.68 per 100 pounds but $2.47 per 100 pounds. I would love to have the hon. member for St. Boniface justify that.
Let me take another product used in the iron and steel industry, skelp. To ship 100 pounds of skelp from Hamilton to Vancouver, you pay $1.35 per 100 pounds. To ship the same 100 pounds of skelp from Hamilton to Edmonton, a distance substantially shorter than from Hamilton to Vancouver, you pay $2.11 per 100 pounds. There you have another example of why western Candians, regardless of party, are unhappy with the present transportation policy.
For a moment let me try to sum up by suggesting to the minister, who said we had not really explained what we mean by a national transportation policy, that we believe a national transportation policy must be related to an efficient and adequate transportation system that makes the best use of all available forms of transportation; railroads, ships, airlines, buses and pipelines. All these are essential to the economic and social well-being and growth of Canada. All these should be studied with a view to integration in order that they may be used to the best

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
advantage. In this way competition, which now acts unevenly in various parts of Canada and between smaller and larger users of transportation facilities, would be equalized. A national policy demands that all regions of Canada must develop to their maximum potential, and a national transportation act should have that as its fundamental purpose.
Let me conclude with one suggestion to the present minister, who was the minister responsible for the greatest expansion and expenditure under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. We have spent hundreds of millions of dollars put up by the Canadian taxpayers to bring industry to have-not areas. To a large extent, we have brought them through a helter-skelter policy based on a principle that escapes me and other members. We have brought industry to areas where, under the present system, they cannot pay transportation costs and, as a result, will not in the foreseeable future be viable operations.
Let me make this suggestion to the minister, and I do so after thorough discussion with one of the best economists in this country. The best thing we could do would be to wipe out the whole program of grants under regional economic expansion, as well as under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. We are now giving tens of millions of dollars to new industry in have-not areas. The money saved could be directed toward offsetting the cost of transportation so that industry in areas long distances from the markets could produce and deliver products as cheaply as they are now produced in Toronto, Hamilton and Montreal. If that were the main purpose of our national transportation policy, instead of helping those who need help the least, as we are now doing, the people in western Canada would not be as dissatisfied, justifiably so, with the present national transportation policy and the present government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before this House touches upon a matter of tremendous importance to western Canada, and it is largely for that reason I want to say a few words about it today. The very foundations of this country, and the very introduction to it in a firm way of western Canada, were closely associated with certain transportation policies being developed with a view to the nature of the country and the nature of the relationship which would exist between the new areas, the new territories and the earlier settled part of the country. From that day to this the issue of transportation has been very high on the list of any westerner talking about problems from a national point of view, and problems which particularly trouble the western region of the country and about which westerners feel unhappy.
The traditional way of approaching this subject by politicians has certainly been to catalogue specific grievances and to examine specific rates and compare them, and not to go much deeper than that into the nature of the transportation system, its cost and the logic or philosophy behind such a system. Too often, partly because the governments in power have not been doing an adequate job of facing up to western needs in relation to the transportation system, opposition members of parliament have taken the loud route in point to problems and difficulties, usual-

ly reciting them in long lists without bothering to pay attention to the fact that the solutions to some of their problems would only increase other problems to which they are pointing.
I do not complain about that activity in the sense that it is not expected of opposition, but it is a fact that governments from the earlier establishment of national policy to this day have not adequately been able to develop a form or variation of transportation policy which seems satisfactory to the west. It has always been the view of the westerner that the government was attempting to run with or maintain a particular policy, and opposition members were pointing this out. Perhaps that explains why, historically, me prairie provinces in particular have traditionally oeeii so heavily represented in tin. opposition, no matter which government was in power, rather than on the government side of the House.
The significant thing is that this government at this time is determined to come to grips with this problem honestly and squarely. That is the real significance of the western economic opportunities conference, both in relation to transportation, which must loom large on the scene, and in relation to certain other specific items on the conference agenda such as economic development, industrial development and the nature of our agricultural life in the west.
These other items are important and, indeed, transportation is only important as it relates to the people who live in the west, the products that may be produced or found in the west, the way in which they may be moved and the way in which this may provide jobs. Transportation does not exist for itself alone, but for the people and the products it can carry and serve. That is the important thing for us to bear in mind as we approach this major question of developing a national policy for the west. We must bear in mind that a transportation policy is not just for transportation but for industry and economic development, for agriculture and processing development and for the kind of life the people of the west want and think they ought to be able to have within this great country of Canada, and of which they want to share a full part.
The simple listing of problems often ignores the realities behind the existing situation. A railroad expert can explain why, on occasion, longer haul rates may be lower than shorter haul rates. He can explain why the longer conveying would be lost all together to the railroad if it were not at a lower rate. He could explain that the higher rate is needed where it can be obtained in order to cover whatever basic costs are said must be borne by the railroads. Of course, that is a fundamental principle for national decision; that is, what proportion of the total cost ought to be borne in respect of freight and people, and what proportion ought to be borne by the treasury of this country instead of by freight and people.
This is a fundamental question and one which has been examined exhaustively by royal commissions with a cer-iain conclusion and certain direction in them. The Mac-Pherson Commission looked at this problem, that if you have a situation where freight is being carried at below total cost, then there is a good argument for other freight
June 19, 1973

not to bear that cost but for it to be borne by the treasury generally. Of course, in connection with branch lines and grain moving over the branch lines, we now feel the fruits of that policy in the form of large sums of money being paid the railways to cover what would otherwise be losses on that grain, thus avoiding the charging of higher rates to other classes ot freight moving on tne railways. That really is one ot tne fundamental problems I believe m the competitive control policy which the MacPherson Royal Commission seemed to think was so desirable and reasonable. The problem was that, over the years, if any product was not bearing its full share of the total cost of the rail operation, then the railways looked to the other products which they were carrying, whether people or freight, to attempt if possible to obtain an offset against the losses on that product. That is a very important decision that is made by the railways, and one which must be reviewed and examined by a government as a part of the review of our national policy.
What we really need is a constant examination of the relationship between freight rates, between freight rates on grain and freight rates on meat, to see what happens when you have this discrepancy in the way those rates are approached, or between freight rates on unprocessed materials and freight rates on processed materials, in the light of whatever our national policy may be in relation to where those materials ought to be processed and what ought to be encouraged in this country. That is the procedure we are following. We are following it not with another royal commission but with an intensive examination with our own resources and on the facts which are certainly available to us. This is the approach which we thought had to be taken with regard to branch lines and the grain movement. Opposition members simply rise and say, do not abandon the branch lines. They look at two years of studies which we have and they make very little comment on them, perhaps because we have not treated them as proposals upon which we wanted to stand without full consultation with producers. We wanted to examine the problem and lay the facts of this particular part of rail operations before the people.
What I think we cannot afford is unnecessary expenditures which do not serve a useful purpose, whether they are borne by the payer of the freight or by the treasury generally. That does not make sense and that is why we must look critically at these things. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) talks about stopping abandonment of branch lines. He knows full well that an Order in Council has stopped any significant exercise in that regard, and that furthermore, essentially branch lines have not been abandoned as a result of whatever procedure exists in the Canadian Transportation Commission for hearings in that regard. What has been happening has been that in some cases the very users of the lines have been abandoning them. People have been moving from rail to truck to move most of their products, and in some cases grain companies themselves have been leaving a rail line to consolidate their operations somewhere else. The users have been abandoning the branch lines, but the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre would have them all remain forever as a monument no doubt for the payment of treasury money to the rail system for some reason I do not understand.
Transportation Policy
I say to the hon. member most seriously that when he takes that stand of defending to the last every branch line and wants some expenditure on them, however wasteful that may be, he is doing a disservice to the cause of finding a logical and legitimate national transportation policy. Of course we know, and we have said so repeatedly, that the implications of any change in that regard upon the people affected by it is an important part of the determination of what action should be taken. We started studies on the community impact of any change which might be made, even though this is logically and largely a part of the function of the provincial government involved in the area. We have involved them in our discussions in order that they be fully associated with any decisions which are taken.
Hon. members are fond of saying simply, let us make use of the Port of Churchill. They ignore the fact that the Canadian Wheat Board record in relation to the Port of Churchill is outstanding. In recent years, record movements of grain, two years of top movements, have gone through the Port of Churchill as a result of the facilities which are there. Hon. members say, let us use the facilities more. There is no suggestion that we should make a cost analysis or determine whether an extra $10 million spent there on new facilities is in fact more or less useful than a $10 million facility erected, say, at Robert's Bank or, an additional facility in Prince Rupert or in some other location.
Those, however, are the hard questions which a responsible government must ask. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, a member of the New Democratic Party which had a government in Saskatchewan for a number of years at different times and in Manitoba at the moment, does not ask what those governments do to encourage the flow of freight through Churchill. Why is it that the freight going through Churchill is, in fact, in the order of 90 per cent or 95 per cent grain, Wheat Board initiated, and not initiated in any way by the provincial government to encourage the use of the port. The fact is that we have been examining this port very closely and we have been its best supporter.
In this reasoned situation, we must recognize the shortness of the length of the season at that port under certain circumstances and must judge expenditures of money in that light. Hon. members say we should use the port more. In the last negotiations with the Russians the Wheat Board received a firm commitment from them to make use of the port of Churchill for the first time in order to move some grain. As a result I have a letter here from Mr. Willis Richford, President of the Hudson Bay Route Association. He says:
Dear Mr. Lang:
On behalf of myself and the Hudson Bay Route Association I would like to convey congratulations to you, and to your officials involved, concerning the recently announced sale of grains to Russia, and especially for the announcement that some of it will move through Churchill. We hope that this return of Russian to Churchill is but the first of yearly visits to that port.
To that I say, amen. It expresses indeed our view of the usefulness of this port and how we ought to try to make use of it to the full. But, of course, we must look at costs. Hon. members say we should make more use of Prince Rupert. Of course, they do not point to the fact that the

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
number of bushels of grain going through Prince Rupert moved from under 12 million bushels in 1970-71 to 14 million bushels in 1971-72, and with the additional facilities put in place for this year, the amount is already
26,600,000	bushels. It may go as high as 30 million bushels in the course of the year. Hon. members perhaps do not know that Prince Rupert, and the people in that area, recognize the efforts which have been made to use the elevator and, in the process of making record sales, to use it in record proportion. I have a letter here from Mr. W. J. Scott, the Chairman of the Port Development Commission of the city of Prince Rupert. It reads:
Dear Mr. Lang:
It has been most gratifying the past few months to see the increased use being made of the local Canadian government elevator. We realize that this is the result of the efforts of yourself, and the many other officials responsible for grain movement and are most appreciative.
The large volume of grain being handled here demonstrates and confirms the capacity and efficiency of the local plant, and we hope that it will continue to be used to the same degree.
Mr. Speaker, the plain fact is that we have been able to more volumes of grain that no one thought of before. By planning ahead now, we are looking at the development of a policy for the west which can make a positive contribution to the future of the west for years to come.
There has been some discussion about whether we will have positive proposals. The facts are that this government has launched an intensive effort to determine the nature of the problems and possible solutions of western problems in the short and in the long-run. That means we will not be happy if we stop with patching particular problems to which the finger has been pointed over the years. I, as a western member of the government, and my colleagues will not be content unless we in fact continue the work we are now doing in solving specific problems, solving some of them indeed in the very short run. But I will not be content unless we develop the kind of approach and philosophy to the needs of western Canada which will affect and influence national policy on many fronts during many years to come.
That is what I had occasion to say a few days ago in Winnipeg and it has been the subject of certain comment since then. Mr. Speaker, I have since had occasion to see a newspaper headline and, as a result, I understand why the provincial premiers are a little sensitive. It was a headline which implied that I was scolding the western premiers. I do not think that was really the gist of my speech. What I was really doing was indicating to them that the western opportunities conference could bog down if a short-term view or a petty partisan, political view were taken of it; that that had to be seriously avoided, and that this was an opportunity such as the west had never had in terms of modern development of national policy for it.
The comments I made before making that speech-the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) was wrong, as usual, because so far as I can recall I did not talk to any members of the press after the speech, but only before it- were to the effect that I was optimistic. I admit that I sounded the warning because I thought it important that we avoid political pot-shotting and I was optimistic that

this view would be taken by the western premiers. Notwithstanding that, I think it a little strange that the word "scolding" was used. However, Mr. Speaker, I reserve the right to scold a premier from time to time. It seems strange that there are no rules or limits at all on what a western premier may say about me or one of my colleagues in this House, but they show a certain sensitivity if some comment is made by me against them.
I am grateful, and I am sure my colleagues are, for the advice that hon. members tendered today and yesterday both to my colleagues and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). They have tried; they have shown their great earnestness. They wanted the government to know what a liability I am in this connection and how well the government will perform if something different is done to me, or with me, or for me. I am sure they are earnest in their efforts to have the government in a strong position. I know that is their motivation and I, for one, appreciate it.
Over the years I have become quite used to being one of the several lone rangers of the House in this area. But this is a moment when I am deeply proud to be a western member of this government, a government which-and hon. members cannot challenge it-has shown determination at last, after years of neglect, to do something that is basic to the national policy of this country as it relates to western Canada. A Conservative opposite says, "Right." Of course, the point is that while his party was last in power, with a western prime minister and a solid phalanx of western members from the Prairies, they did nothing of a fundamental nature for the west. What they did, Mr. Speaker, was to offer the very kind of petty palliatives that I was warning about a few moments ago.
Let us not talk in terms of solving western policy problems by building a post office in Podunk. When the Conservative government was in power, not only did it take total pride in building a post office in Podunk but its members took special pride in it since they said it really showed a western Tory heart, because Podunk didn't even need a post office. That is not the role that this government seeks.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I hope hon. members will not see it as a hopeless political admission if I say that I do not expect all the problems that relate to the development of a national policy for western Canada will be solved by July 26. But I firmly believe this is the first time a government has taken hold of the problem with real determination to do something about it. I expect western Canada to understand that and to work together with us to see that new development of a national policy comes about.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past several months the government has firmly committed itself to a policy of industrial decentralization within Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) have both talked at great length on the need to develop secondary industry in the west adjacent to the region's great resource and energy base. Certainly these are admirable intentions and it is hoped that the government will actively pursue policies designed to promote industrial development in western Canada. The upcoming conference on western economic opportunity will demonstrate
June 19, 1973

just how sincere is the government in its intention to alleviate one of the most important problems confronting the western provinces.
One industry in Manitoba which could use a great deal of government promotion and assistance is the aerospace industry. Since the departure of the Air Canada overhaul base from Winnipeg to Dorval in 1969, the Manitoba aviation industry has floundered as successive Liberal governments have failed to honour their commitments to that industry. Air Canada's successor at the Winnipeg base, CAE Aircraft, has been beset with difficulties ever since it took over the operation. Lack of work has resulted in tremendous financial losses, and the company currently employs but a mere handful of people. Government contracts or assistance have not been forthcoming and as a result the aerospace industry in Manitoba is slowly dying. However, the industry's demise really began with the transfer of the overhaul facility to Dorval.
The transfer of the overhaul base to Dorval was probably one of the worst decisions ever made by a Liberal government-and there have been many bad decisions. The move destroyed what was once a viable industry in Manitoba and is partially responsible for making Air Canada an even more inefficient airline than ever before. In the interest of industrial decentralization, increased efficiency and safety, the government should take the necessary steps to move portions of the overhaul base back to Winnipeg. The facilities are still there, and there is a definite desire among the employees transferred to Dorval to move back to Winnipeg.
The problems at Dorval are monumental, and if practices there are an indication of the manner in which Air Canada is being administered then it is time for a complete investigation of that corporation. The recent strike and the numerous walkouts by Air Canada employees in recent years suggest that such a full scale investigation might be necessary. There are many contentious issues still be to resolved between Air Canada and the unions, and such as inquiry might pinpoint the reasons for the many continuing problems. For example, the use of strike breakers by Air Canada to perform the work functions of striking employees in the Winnipeg finance branch does little to enhance labour-management relations. In any case, an investigation into the happenings at Dorval is certainly warranted.
I have written to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) several times outlining why such an investigation is needed. I have also raised the matter in committee. The minister refuses to act. And while Air Canada officials have invited me to Dorval to inspect premises I have inspected twice before, they appear reluctant to investigate the malpractices which I have called to their attention. Should the minister undertake to examine the Dorval situation I am sure he would arrive at conclusions similar to those I am about to discuss.
Mr. J. R. Baldwin, the current president of Air Canada, said that the transfer was made in the interests of increased efficiency, economy and operating effectiveness. I assert, however, that Air Canada in Dorval is neither economically more viable nor more operationally efficient
Transportation Policy
than it was in Winnipeg. In fact, the opposite is true. I base my comments upon both my own investigation and information afforded me by employees. More specific details in relation to the charges I am about to make can only be provided by the employees themselves. Obviously, this would require a situation whereby they could be assured of immunity, but I can guarantee that several persons, many of whom have retired early because of the situation at Dorval, would be only too happy to appear before any investigative body studying the situation.
Air Canada at Dorval is highly overstaffed in some departments and grossly understaffed in others. In some areas this lack of staff results in failure to comply with MOT regulations. This fact has serious implications in relation to safety on Air Canada planes. It has also been brought to my attention that certain safety regulations in the avionics overhaul shop in Dorval do not comply with MOT regulations. The specifications laid down relative to quality audits are ignored, and there is no inspector in the shop.
I am also told that outdated systems which are responsible for much inefficiency are in widespread use. Employee morale is low at Dorval, especially among the 234 drafted Manitobans. As well, performance levels of both equipment and personnel is so poor as to stagger the imagination. Furthermore, there is little research activity being undertaken by Air Canada at Dorval. Basic training for employees is non-existent and many are unaware of MOT standards, requirements or even general procedures.
Tremendous and unnecessary costs are being accrued by Air Canada at Dorval. For example, a plethora of useless publications are printed and distributed every week. Each publication has its own staff, materials and distribution costs to pay. Officials at Dorval have told me that there is no real effort made by administrators to obtain MOT required manuals which are necessary to familiarize employees with particular subjects. I have also been informed that rejected equipment, particularly worn out tires, are being used on certain aircraft. One has to wonder what kind of safety regulations are being adhered to when this is allowed to occur.
As I mentioned earlier, these are but a few of the problems. Meanwhile, the facilities in Winnipeg remain for the most part unused. By moving portions of the air maintenance base back to Winnipeg the government would not only be demonstrating its sincerity with regard to its policy of industrial decentralization, but would be acting to partially remedy a dangerous situation. It is imperative that the Minister of Transport give his utmost consideration to the facts I have just mentioned.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the comparison between the two cabinet ministers who participated in the debate this afternoon. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has obviously become a linguistic psychotic with a phobia in that field, rather than being an expert in transportation. I was interested in his reference to Doug Fisher. Although I am unaware of the article to which he referred, I have known Mr. Fisher for a number of years. When he was in this House he was considered to be an expert on transportation and was offered a number of jobs in the labour management field and in the administration field by both our

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
national transportation systems. I think it is doubtful, Mr. Speaker, that the present minister will be in this ministry long enough to learn half of what Mr. Fisher has forgotten about transportation.
I had hoped that the Minister of Transport would be open to suggestion for the development of a national transportation system. This is very important to all parts of Canada and not only northern Ontario. But it is so important there that the Premier of Ontario, like his colleagues in western Canada, has decided that the federal government is failing its responsibility, particularly in regard to rail transportation. It has been decided that the province of Ontario must do something about equalizing costs in various parts of the country, and that government recently announced that it will cut freight rates in northern Ontario by 18 per cent. The premier said this reduction would be made on a number of selected commodities and that it was not intended to continue the program long followed by North American railways of restricting any advantages in this field to raw materials. In an article in the Globe and Mail the premier is quoted as saying:
-the 30-day period would also be used for consultation with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways on rates in areas where mutual action will be necessary. There has been no prior consultation with CPR or CNR, one of the premier's aides said.
The government will reduce freight rates to and from northern Ontario in two ways. First, by slashing ONR rates, thereby lowering the over-all rate for a shipment into or out of the north which connects with the CPR or CNR.
Second, by cutting the rates charged by Star Transfer, the ONR's trucking arm. Star Transfer connects directly with Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, for a long time the province of Ontario has been concerned with the problems of northern Ontario and its inability to set rates for freight coming in there, these being set in the main by the Canadian National Railways operating out of Toronto. I was interested in the most recent report of the Canadian Transport Commission which is a regulatory body. With reference to passenger service on the Toronto-North Bay-Kapuskasing line a loss of $1,315,113 was indicated, the amount of the certified loss was $1,186,521, and the payment by the federal government to the CNR was $949,217.
On numerous occasions, Mr. Speaker, the Ontario government has offered to buy that line and a few years ago was willing to pay $2 million for it, so I presume it would not be unreasonable to offer $10 million now for the line from Toronto to North Bay. Every citizen in Canada is paying a million dollars a year for passenger service, and if the CNR thinks it is such a liability it could sell that particular line to the Ontario Northland Railway. It could be operated into Toronto, and I am sure it would make a profit.
Why do so few people travel by train, Mr. Speaker? A short while ago my wife booked a bedroom from Toronto to New Liskeard, You get on the train in Toronto in the evening, and get off at New Liskeard at four o'clock in the morning. My wife bought the thing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: The whole thing?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
When I say she bought it, I means she paid so much for it for one night. These old cars were bought from the American railways for $2,000. She paid $28 for the use of that berth from Toronto to New Liskeard. You could go to pretty nearly any hotel in Toronto and sleep all night in comfortable surroundings for less than $28, which is what she paid for her accommodation in an old car which was thrown away by the American railway, not one or two years ago but 14 or 15 years ago. We picked up all the old junk from the American railways. So we are not running a passenger service to meet the needs of the people. If you are travelling the 400 miles to Toronto, there is no point in driving; it is more advantageous to go by train. You get on the train at night, sleep on the train, arrive at your destination, do your business in the day, get back on the train, sleep all night, and get off in the morning. That is how people used to do it. They do not necessarily do it any longer.
Also, consider the mail situation. At one time, if a letter was posed in Toronto at about four o'clock in the afternoon, it was in your mail-box in New Liskeard at eight o'clock the next morning. Now it takes five days, if you are lucky. Occasionally I am surprised when mail arrives in one day. Sometimes, however, it takes three weeks, and on occasion I have received mail that has arrived more than 30 days after posting. That is how long it has taken to go 375 miles. So we are not running trains for people; we are running trains for the railways. The Ontario government, in making its concession, should not be thwarted because Canadian National Railways say there is to be an increase of 6 per cent increase on certain categories of freight going to northern Ontario.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who is responsible for the Wheat Board, just finished speaking. He was very upset because some newspapers had reported his arrogance. The premiers of western Canada are aware of his arrogance and they resent his making the statements attributed to him. If the government hopes to solve the transportation problem in western Canada in the same way as we hope to solve it in northern Ontario, there must be co-operation among all forms of transportation. Arrogance is not good enough.
What did the minister say in his speech? He was kind enough to make a copy of the speech available to us. Among other things, in western Canada the old Crowsnest rate structure may come under review. If the Crowsnest rate structure in western Canada comes under review, the only thing that can happen is that the rate will go down. It runs as high as 24 cents in one area of Saskatchewan, and goes down as one travels to the terminals either on the west coast or at the head of the lakes. The minister suggests it may come under review. What he is really telling people is this, "You had better agree to the proposal I am going to make or we will eliminate the Crowsnest pass rate which has been sacrosanct for many years."
When you consider a national transportation policy, no element can be taken by itself. The Minister of Transport today talked about STOL aircraft. I heard some nonsense from Air Canada the other day, when I was at Earlton, about that airline dropping its regional service. It will go as far as Earlton at least, I take it, and allow Norontair to take over. But that is another story. Norontair is an airline
June 19, 1973

established by the provincial government to operate in northern Ontario with three Beaver aircraft.
Obviously, short take-off and landing facilities will be provided in a number of communities, but we have lost our national carrier. This, of course, has happened in other areas. Our transportation system was considered a few years ago and it was decided that there would be regional carriers and Nordair, not Norontair, would serve this northern area. What did Nordair do? Nordair obtained permission to fly between Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal. It has the lucrative end of the market and does not need to worry about supplying feeder line service.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Don't forget Hamilton.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Also, TransAir has moved from western Canada, Winnipeg, to Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie and Toronto. Of course, it wants to fly to Toronto without any intermediate stops. At the same time, we really do need a regional air service.
It is time we sat down and discussed this whole area. We should not just deal with present rates. The Minister of Transport, if he lives to be a thousand, will never be smart enough to understand how all these rates were developed. Such an exercise, in any event, would be futile and probably impossible. There are literally thousands of rates which affect various commodities, and they vary with area, zone and all kinds of conditions. We should get rid of those rates and set a number of standard rates that would be effective on either a regional or a national basis. They should be related, as the minister suggested, to the cost of moving a passenger or of moving goods. We should relate these rates to the cost of the operation of the transportation facility.
If we were to do that and relate these rates to the other services involved, we would find that transportation in this country would need to be on a national basis. The system must be integrated; we must unite all the major forms of transportation. Certainly there is no justification for two major airlines and the various regional carriers. There is no justification for two national railways and no justification, obviously, for all the PCV licences and the trucking concerns that are attached to the other forms of transportation in this nation.
There should be an integrated transportation system. The matter of transportation is the major problem in northern Ontario, as has been said at every conference held by every government, every municipality and every agency that has considered the problem. I am sure there is an identical problem in the Manumes and, judging by what members from western Canada say, there is a similar problem in western Canada. It is one that we ought to face.
When we decided that the Canadian Transport Commission, and not parliament, should be given power to control and regulate in this field, we erred; we were wrong. It is not possible to give a regulatory body the authority to create an integrated transportation system for this nation. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, that question should be brought back to parliament and parliament should again consider an integrated national transportation policy that will serve the needs of this nation to the advantage of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the six o'clock recess, I was indicating that Canada needs a transportation policy that fully integrates all forms of transportation. The Canadian Transport Commission which was established to regulate the various forms of transportation has been a total failure in developing any kind of integrated service. It is my guess that neither this government nor the official opposition will be able to develop the type of transportation facilities necessary for this country within the next 50 years.
Most Canadians will agree that the railways should remain an integral part of our transportation system. They will also agree that Canadian National and Canadian Pacific must be united to rationalize the rail transportation system across this country. It is stupid to have a half empty train travelling half a mile behind another half empty train and the government paying a subsidy for those lines.
It may be necessary for the provinces to operate some form of rail transportation system. For this reason, I will make the offer, on behalf of the Ontario government, to buy the line from North Bay to Toronto. I am sure the Ontario minister of communications would agree to a $10 million payment, and if necessary he would probably double that figure. We are now paying $1 million a year for passenger service lines. This fact should encourage the minister to project his policies for at least ten years and allow the sale of that particular line so that northern Ontario can be united with southern Ontario.
Unless this government considers an integrated transportation policy there are a number of things it will not be able to do. It will be necessary to determine the most economic, efficient and effective type of service for all segments of Canada, including rail, air and ground transportation. Canada is 20, 30 or more years behind in providing rapid transit service. Japan has a train which can travel at 300 miles an hour with relative safety.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Two hundred.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
My friend says it is 200 miles an hour. It is interesting to note that during World World II, New York Central operated the Silver Bullet through part of Canada at an average speed of 90 miles an hour. That was more than 30 years ago. If the New York Central could do that at that time, I do not think I am too far out in my guess of 300 miles an hour for the train in Japan. Such a service would advantageously affect our airport development and urban centres. In a film on television the other night it was pointed out that our urban development is on a five-year basis. Scientists in this field stated that urban transportation systems should be considered for 50 or 100-year

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
periods. In the municipal field we are really operating on a five-year program.
The federal government must take a very serious look at the total transportation situation. They must relate one service to another. As my colleagues have pointed out, there is no point having a STOL aircraft service between Ottawa and Montreal and having to spend more time getting to and from the airports here and in Ste Scholas-tique or Dorval than it takes a train to travel from downtown Ottawa to downtown Montreal even with the inefficiencies of CPR and CNR.
There is also the matter of economics. We reached the peak of inefficiency in this country when we put pollution controls on automobiles. In an ideal situation this will cut out 50 per cent of the pollution. However, it has doubled the gasoline consumption. There is no efficiency whatsoever. We would be better off driving a 1965 automobile, with no pollution controls, than a 1973 model with pollution controls. With a 50 per cent reduction in pollution, over a three-year period the exhaust pollution emitted would be exactly the same.
I do not fault the transport commission in this regard. They have failed in many other fields, but I do not think this is their responsibility. It is the responsibility of members of parliament and of governments. I hope the minister will prove me wrong, but I believe an NDP government will have to come to power in Ottawa before we see a satisfactory, over-all transportation policy in operation across this country covering movement by air, ground and water to serve the needs of all and equalize opportunity for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the applause will be as warm at the end of my remarks.
It is worth noting how little interest this debate seems to raise on the motion moved by the New Democratic Party, particularly the opposition parties. Obviously, when one hears as many pessimistic and negative expressions of opinion, it is difficult to raise much interest in this Chamber.
Mr. Speaker, the opposition motion now before us gives me the opportunity to speak once again on a subject matter that is most important for the area I represent in this House, namely the matter of transport. If I may, I shall make some remarks on the condition of transport in general in the Atlantic area, or in Eastern Canada if you wish.
The tenor of the motion under study, which aims at -greater use of the Ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert, -provides us with an opportunity to make some observations on the proposed development of deep-water ports in the Riviere-du-Loup region, which is so dear to the heart of my colleague from Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron).
The problem of transportation, particularly with regard to rates and grants, is a most complex one. To attempt to solve the problem by developing a new national transpor-

tation policy, as the text of today's motion says, will not necessarily lead us-to borrow the words of the distinguished Prime Minister of India, Mrs. Gandhi, who honoured us with her visit today-to a real solution, namely one which will not lead to other problems caused in turn by the adoption of temporary solutions.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) made reference in his speech to a policy for the equalization of transportation rates, against which he warned us, particularly of the danger to the Atlantic provinces inherent in this formula. The formula in question is one which would discourage new manufacturing industries from setting up business here, and the same applies to western Canada, since the formula will simply help large manufacturing companies in central Canada to penetrate these markets, and not to establish themselves there, as is hoped for.
It may be, as the New Democratic Part claims, that Canada needs to change its national transportation policy. I will not deny this altogether, for I am not an expert, and moreover I do not believe that there are any real experts in this field, any more than in any other field of political or economic activity in this country.
We must also yield to the facts and admit that the political party of the proposer of this motion must also, from time to time, revise its proposals for solutions and take into account the rapid and constant change which is characteristic of the transportation sector. It is obviously a constantly evolving field and if there is an aspect of the question which must hold our attention further, it is precisely the current vitality of the transportation industry and the concern with which Canadian companies seize all opportunities to turn them to account for the great benefit of Canada in general.
In spite of all that, there remain specific regions and activity sectors which do not evolve as fast as the demand in the transportation service sector, where, as it happens in the Atlantic region in particular, the transportation industry has not quite reached the service quality that the citizens of that area are entitled to ask for.
Mr. Speaker, the citizens of the "Republic of Madawas-ka"-which by the way is celebrating this year the centenary of its designation as a provincial county-are in a particularly good position to take bearings. In Madawaska, and more particularly in my city of Edmundston, we are practically on that frontier which separates the Atlantic region from what is commonly called central Canada and in which I include Quebec and Ontario, and of course our attention is especially attracted towards central Canada because we are more aware of its presence. Yet, because of our political situation we also belong to the Atlantic region; we are from the Maritimes in Madawaska. So it often happens that conflicts regarding the transportation policy arise and are discussed here.
But we, in Madawaska, believe that people from the Maritimes moan too much over their fate, and that they should more often make constructive, permanent and acceptable proposals to the federal government in Ottawa.
If the federal government sometimes has difficulty in understanding or in accepting the position of the Atlantic region's spokesmen, it is because they have not always
June 19, 1973

come to the federal government with the broadness of mind required or with concrete and practical solutions.
I have still fresh in mind, Mr. Speaker, the unfortunately negative and depressing talks of the New Brunswick premier when he came last week before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to express the position of his government regarding the federal legislation for the screening of foreign investments in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Saint John-Lancas-ter (Mr. Bell) wants to speak, let him in turn rise to make a speech. By the way, I noticed that he was present last week when the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs met; neither he nor his three colleagues opened their mouths to direct questions to the premier of New Brunswick. Are we to infer that they automatically condone the negative and backward position of the premier of New Brunswick? Yes, Mr. Speaker.
A provincial premiei may speak on behalf of my hon. friend's party, but when he suggests that he is speaking on behalf of all the citizens of a province, he should refrain from adopting extreme positions which, to quote his words, can be summarized as follows: The best policy is not to have any.
Mr. Speaker, such a position is utterly unacceptable. Such a stand is unacceptable to New Brunswickers and I need not give any details. The New Brunswick premier represents a certain majority, but he does not represent all the citizens of that province; I contend that I also speak for a sector of New Brunswick, a progressive sector, a sector that wants us to tackle in a realistic way the problems that face us.
It seems to me that when the day comes when provincial government leaders will stop making politics at the expense of the federal government in the hope of getting a momentary election benefit, and that the accredited spokesmen will also be willing to accept the compromise in the federative system, then, Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic area will progress more rapidly than it has done up to now.
I am one of those who never hesitated to criticize certain national transportation companies when it had to be done, but I always tried at the same time to present some kind of solution. Today, one must recognize the lead of the Canadian National Railways over many competitors as regards to rapid container transportation for instance. The result of all that is a blooming activity in the port of Saint-Jean-the port of the colleague opposite who just
Transportation Policy
interrupted me-and all that endeavour is done with the constructive co-operation of the federal government. That is surely something to be proud of.
But in the field of passenger transportation, I must share at times the opinion of my opponents, for that is the grievance of many members in this House.
I stated at the outset that I would comment on the proposed construction of a deep-water port in the Riviere-du-Loup area. I might surprise some members if I confirmed today that north-western New Brunswick and even north-eastern Maine support the Gros-Cacouna project and yet, such is the case. The "Madawaska Republic", Mr. Speaker, 80 miles south of Riviere-du-Loup, has supported the promoters of that project from the early 50's, because we believe this project would bring beneficial results not only for the people of the Lower St. Lawrence, but also for northwestern New Brunswick and northern Maine.
I think it is important that tne Quebec government and the federal government immediately agree to complete the work undertaken at Gros-Cacouna several years ago, at a cost of several million dollars.
The member for the constituency next to mine, my good friend, the member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata has always earnestly advocated supported the Gros-Cacouna project and from the beginning, well-meaning citizens of the "Madawaska Republic" have joined their efforts to his and again today, the member for Madawaska-Victoria gives his entire support to the member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata and to his likeable neighbours in the Lower St. Lawrence.
Some might say that Madawaska should stay out of this. Madawaska is in New Brunswick, while Gros-Cacouna is in Quebec. Let us say that there is a provincial boundary between the two. But historically, we are closer to Riviere-du-Loup than to St. John or Halifax. It is a fact! And perhaps our natural vocation is to follow the St. John River to the port of the same name. But we have been protaging in Riviere-du-Loup for quite some time.
The port of Gros-Cacouna does not take any thing from St. John, Halifax or Canso. We have been doing that portage for two centuries and we will keep going to Riviere-du-Loup as long as it will be profitable for us to do so.
Some hon. members would like to blame the pollution of the St. Lawrence River on Riviere-du-Loup, a pollution which is flowing down from the Great Lakes through Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec. This pollution is now blamed on Riviere-du-Loup. For ecological and environmental reasons, they want to prevent the supertankers from calling at Gros-Cacouna.
Those are false accusations and I want to denounce them.
A year ago the Stockholm Convention on human environment recognized the principle that under-developed countries should not be deprived of the legitimate development of their resources solely for environmental considerations. Unfortunately, I have not been able to find this document before rising tonight, but I am quoting from it generally. We should retain especially of this principle that the developed and polluted nations cannot slow down the development of under-developed nations on the basis

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
of such considerations. It seems to me that this parallel applies exactly to Canada. It is time that the developped regions give a break to the underdevelopped ones. It is time to give Eastern Quebec and Northern New Brunswick the opportunity to develop, and Gros-Cacouna is a valid argument in favour of this development.
Mr. Speaker, I referred, at the beginning of my speech, to the whimpering that is heard regularly in the Atlantic region, concerning all matters connected with transportation. In spite of all this, some real progress is being achieved and some improvements can be noticed at times. Most recently, on April 9, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) have met with the premiers of the Atlantic provinces. They have agreed on several points and it is useful to repeat them tonight. For instance, they have agreed to grant more assistance to the movement of manufactured and farm products of the Atlantic region toward the markets of Central Canada. And since them, Mr. Speaker, representatives of the federal and provincial governments have worked together to establish the basic rules of such a program and, to solve a few administrative problems, it has been decided that it is of utmost importance to consult the Atlantic area carriers before going further.
I am told that the provincial governments are now altogether prepared to issue in the regional papers a notice to indicate what those basic rules should be and to ask the carriers of the area to make their views known as to the commodities they would like to see included in that program. After those consultations, officers of both levels of government will prepare a list, as complete as possible, of the commodities and then recommend the amount of the supplementary grant, and I too, Mr. Speaker, want to emphasize, as did the Minister of Transport this afternoon, the fact that it is a supplementary grant which applies over and above the existing grant of 30 per cent which is already given in all the Atlantic area up to Quebec City.
Why then should anyone say, that this government has done nothing or is doing nothing to bring about solutions to ever increasing problems.
Then, it will also be recommended, in order not to distort the function of land transportation within the whole pattern, that this increased financing should also be granted to the trucking industry.
In view of the fact that there seems to be a waste of funds in the implementation of the present financing program for regional transportation, that there is abuse in this area or that financing is granted in those cases where they are not really necessary, and in the hope of making this financing more efficient, officials are also preparing recommendations in that direction.
During this meeting of federal ministers and the premiers of the Atlantic region, the importance of establishing a physical distribution service has also been recognized. That is the name that was given to it. This service will be carrying on a study involving small shippers in the area. It will provide advice relating, for instance, to inventory control, packing, storing, as well as to the choice of the means of transportation.

This is, Mr. Speaker, a useful and concrete action, and I thank the minister for providing me with this information. I have no doubt that this action will benefit the Atlantic region. Of course, we might have, if necessary, to change this formula as well as existing ones, in order to make them always more efficient.
A new national transportation policy is not necessary at all, Mr. Speaker. We must change present methods as necessity arises. The people from the Maritimes are said to have some difficulties to adjust to change. This is not quite so in my riding, but I realize that it is a fact in other parts of the Atlantic region. So these people will have to make a special effort to adjust to the rules which have been or will be agreed upon very shortly by the premiers of the Atlantic provinces, with the cooperation of the hon. Minister of Transport and the hon. Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed, since we are discussing transport, to allude ever so briefly to the horse. For a long time, the horse was our best mode of transport. I mention this because, recently, a horse by the name of "Secretariat" won the triple crown in the United States, and a young man from my riding, from my own town, Mr. Ron Turcotte, rode him to three brilliant victories. I am sure my colleagues in this House, regardless of their political affiliation, will want to join me in expressing to Ron Turcotte, his father, mother, brothers, sisters and children, the admiration we feel for his feat.
