subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am in sympathy with the motion before us today, I should have liked it expressed in much stronger terms than a simple suggestion that this House is of the opinion that Canada needs a new national transportation policy. Speaking as a westerner, I should like to express our view as we approach the western economic conference to be held later this summer, specifically in the area of transportation and freight rates. Without doubt, this problem has become the number one issue in western Canada, not simply from the point of view of general interest in the area but because the transportation policy of the present government is militating against the economic development of our area. It militates against that which this government has gone on record as favouring as indicated by its programs of regional economic expansion.
Today we have a transportation policy which is structured for the advantage of those heavily populated areas we generally refer to as the industrial belt. Rising freight rates in western Canada are seriously curtailing economic growth, particularly in areas remote from the manufacturing centres in eastern Canada.
Since 1967 the railway companies have not been required to seek approval of a regulatory body before freight rate increases are imposed. We have had a number of increases since that time. The railways do not have to justify contemplated rate increases to a regulatory body. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) indicated to the railways recently that any contemplated increase would be looked at very critically, particularly in western Canada. This is about the only type of control left, and one wonders how long it will last.
June 19, 1973

I submit very clearly that a national transportation policy must be considered from other than a simple transportation point of view. It must be considered as a factor in the economic development of depressed areas. It must be considered in relation to virtual monopolies in some areas which have resulted from transportation structures, lack of proper rail facilities and problems of distance. Certain areas in western Canada have not been able to develop secondary manufacturing industries because of these monopolies, and as a result have not been able to maintain jobs.
We must develop a policy which will allow the development of a diversified economic base, something which western Canadians would dearly love. Since the time immemorial western Canada has been a supplier of raw materials for eastern Canadian industry. We are now struggling in western Canada in a very determined manner to develop secondary manufacturing and processing industries which will allow us to diversify, thus avoiding further exploitation of our raw materials and agricultural products.
One factor that automatically militates against this development is geographic location; that is to say, distance from existing markets in the more heavily populated areas of Canada. I would suggest the single factor which works against development and diversification in the west is not simply distance. Distance can be overcome, and has been with modern technology. Today we are seeing that freight rates are stacked against us and represent the major obstacle to development and diversification. We are aware of the discrepancy in freight rates, and we do not want more promises; we want change and action. We expect action from this government, particularly in light of the forthcoming western economic conference. We require action that will clearly show we are moving toward a national transportation policy
Those of us who live on the Prairies know it costs less to ship canned goods from Toronto to Vancouver tnan it does from Toronto to Regina. This is a fact of life. But what better area is there than the heartland of western Canada for the development of a secondary, processing industry related specifically to agricultural products?
An Ron. Member: What about northern Ontario?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Northern Ontario is another matter. If we are to develop processing industries directly geared to our agricultural base, how can we do so when our biggest single cost is transportation and when there seems to be very little hope of any change?
Let me give another example. When we haul steel from Hamilton to Vancouver, often destined for the export markets of the Pacific rim, the freight cost per 100 pounds is $1.35. To ship the same amount of steel from Hamilton to Edmonton costs $2.11. Surely this fact militates against what our regional economic expansion programs have tried to do for the development of secondary industry in areas of economic depression and slow growth.
If a monopoly situation exists, I submit that the rail companies have clearly shown us on the Prairies that they will take advantage of the prairie buyer because he is
Transportation Policy
locked into the transportation system. In return, the rail companies automatically say that while we are dealing with Vancouver we must be aware of the Panama Canal and ocean shipping. I suggest that is hardly an automatic answer for those of us who live in the prairie area.
This whole matter of rail rates or freight rates would be more easily accepted if we knew that the rail companies were self-sufficient, that they were on a competitive basis in a free enterprise system and were simply trying to make a profit on the basis of competition. We know, however, that this is not the case. The rail companies have received subsidies. We know that Canadian National Railways is a publicly-owned facility, and therefore as a public facility it should be geared to the betterment of specific areas of Canada. In addition, there should be a national policy of rail transportation which would be national from the Atlantic coast to the Pacific coast of Canada, and not only in those areas where we must be competitive. And I ask, competitive with whom?
This government has spent a great deal of money on regional economic expansion. I shall not go into that matter. A consciousness has developed that secondary or processing industry must develop in areas such as the Maritimes and the Prairies. Grants have been made. Yet what are the facts? Is this really a policy which makes sense, in view of the freight rates which militate against such development? The prairie region is generally known as an agricultural area. In recent years the growing of rapeseed has become a large part of our agricultural base. Let us look at this specialty crop to see how it is handled in Canada today. I have already stated that DREE is specifically interested in this development. One can ship 100 pounds of unprocessed rapeseed from Alberta to Montreal for 81 cents. If it is processed into oil or meal, then the cost of shipping the same amount the same distance is $1.22.
On top of that, DREE makes grants for the establishment of processing industry. Where does DREE make these grants? In eastern Canada. I ask, Mr. Speaker, where should you establish such a plant? Obviously, in the agricultural area which could sustain such a plant and would provide much employment, rather than in the industrial heartland which has already a heavy industrial base.
Therefore, I submit that a national transportation policy is necessary if the policies of the government specifically related to economic expansion are to have a long-term, lasting effect. One simply cannot expect to have transportation in isolation, and economic development in isolation: they are both part of the same parcel.
In this House in the past week we have heard much about airport construction, particularly at Pickering. We have heard about impact studies being conducted, studies which were to look very carefully into the effects of the proposed airport on the surrounding area. What happens when we look at rail line abandonment? Rail lines are just as important to the rural areas of Canada as the proposed airports and airlines are to the industrial heartland.
If rail lines are to be abandoned, what happens? Public hearings are held. People may attend these hearings. Anyone who wishes to speak in relation to rail line abandonment may do so. He may speak about the local situa-

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
tion and the severe effect the rail line abandonment will have on a specific area. He might not have too many facts, but he has the knowledge of a person who has lived in the area and who-knows the situation. However, the rail line executives appear at the hearing with briefs, studies and what-have-you, and by the time they are through one might ask what the point was in having a hearing. One might as well forget it.
As a consequence, it is the rail lines which almost dictate what will happen irrespective of local needs or local input. I suggest that the local people are simply being undercut by the experts. I would ask the experts to take another look at the situation. The farmer in the area knows what the effect will be. He knows that he must now take his grain 10 or 15 miles to the country elevator, and he knows what the effect will be if he must transport it 40 miles. He does not need a study to prove to him what the effect will be.
If rail line abandonment is to be considered-and apparently its consideration is continual-then I suggest impact studies must be considered by the Minister of Transport in order to determine the effect of rail line abandonment on small communities. We should approach such studies, not necessarily from the standpoint of the cost relative to transportation but, rather, from the point of view of whether rail line abandonment is in direct conflict with the economic development of a particular region.
I should like to submit another position relative to this matter. On June 4 and 5 the Hudson Bay Route Association held its annual meeting in connection with the port of Churchill. Churchill is a port to which for many years only lip service has been given in respect of its importance. It is an ocean port which could serve a large part of the prairie region. It could be a real port if the government would give more than lip service to it and would develop it. Only then can it become the port the prairie region needs.
For example, why must a Yorkton builder ship prefabricated homes to Regina, eventually to Montreal and then around the east coast to Churchill, when it would cost much less to place these homes on a train at Yorkton and ship them 700 miles to Churchill? That is hardly a national rail policy. What do we see for the port of Churchill? Very clearly, improvements are needed at the port of Churchill. An infusion of money is required not only at one time but over a period of years so that the port of Churchill could be developed to the extent that it could serve at least the northern part of the Canadian prairies.
Recognition is also needed by the National Harbours Board that the port of Churchill is important. It is necessary that the National Harbours Board place it on the same priority footing as other ports on either coast of Canada. The people of western Canada have a legitimate grievance. We see pressure applied to the present government for feed-freight assistance to eastern livestock producers. Surely adjustments should come in this area. Mr. Speaker, just as adjustments go to the east, so also must we gain a new awareness of the very real grievances in western Canada.

To date, what have we received? We have received no assurances that adjustments will be made to remove freight rate disparities which affect western development. We were given assurances today by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that if we insist, these grievances could be put on the agenda of the western economic conference, but at no time did he specifically say he would be going to that conference to solve these problems in conjunction with the four western premiers. He says, "Oh, yes, we will discuss them; but solutions are another question."
I think the time has come for solutions and not simply for talk. For example, how could the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), speaking recently in Regina and discussing the western economic conference, argue that you cannot prop up one sector of the economy indefinitely at the expense of the rest of the country? How could the Minister of Finance even allude to the fact that the rest of Canada has been propping up the economy of the west, considering present freight rates and the national transportation policy? Such an argument just staggers the imagination. With that type of attitude we will not solve our problems.
For a long time, Mr. Speaker, we in the west have been buying manufactured goods from eastern Canada. We intend to continue to do so. But we want the same assurances, the same protection for western jobs, and a national transportation policy that will protect our interests in the same way as it protects eastern interests and jobs. In our opinion, a new national transportation policy is not only essential but vital to our economic growth. I personally am not, and almost all the people in western Canada are not interested in western alienation. We do not want to feed that horse. We do not want special status. We want equal status, and we will demand equal status on every front where we have a legitimate grievance.
We want the same attention paid to the port of Churchill as is paid to other ports. We want railway executives to give full information on policy respecting the establishment of freight rates. We want them to disclose cost data relative to the use of specific railway areas. We want a closer awareness and an examination of the freight rate policy of the government, specifically as it relates to western Canadian agriculture and to the development of a western economic base.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate that this government has a transportation policy which is continually being adapted to ensure that it is responsive to the needs of the people and of the industry of the country. It is not a national transportation policy as such, but rather it embraces the local, regional, national and international demands of the various social and economic pressures required of its services.
Our transportation systems are flexible in that wherever possible they should be developed on a compatible as well as competitive basis. But while relatively new modes of transportation are being developed, rail and water continue to be the carriers of the bulk of our industrial products, and road and air are the predominant carriers of people. However, in our large urban areas it has become
June 19, 1973

increasingly obvious that the federal government has a major role to play in giving the cities back to the people. This was one of the main reasons bemnd the government's Winnipeg rail study and its intention to present legislation which is designed to increase federal contributions for the removal of railway level crossings.
Being from Manitoba, I have a keen interest in the future of the port of Churchill. I feel that the government is doing much to enhance its economic viability. For example, last April when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) announced the recent sale of wheat and barley to the Soviet Union, he also announced that for the first time the port of Churchill will handle some of the grain shipments to the Soviet Union. The present six-week port of Churchill's shipping season allows it to handle about 22 million bushels, which is the maximum.

speechtext:
In addition, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has directed that further studies be carried out on the future of the port. Present plans include the rebuilding of the wharf and a dredging program designed to allow vessels with deeper draughts access to the port. This is not lip service; these are facts.
The government's local transportation policy is also well reflected in its assistance to the construction of community remote airports. In 1965 the policy was revised to remove the then existing $100,000 ceiling. There was a $1 million limit to the annual funds that were available for these purposes. By January 1, 1972, it became evident that this policy required updating to meet the increasing demands of communities across Canada. A new policy was introduced, increasing the total budget available to $3 million for that year, which enabled the ministry to take care of a backlog of applications. The budget is now $2 million annually. Since the ministry's program of assistance to airport construction and development was begun in 1957-58, up to and including our commitments for the current fiscal year a total of more than $15 million has been spent or is earmarked for expenditure. Of that amount the western provinces have benefited to the extent of nearly $7 million.
In the fiscal year 1972-73, after the new policy of increased assistance came into effect, a total of just under $3 million was committed for 40 projects, of which more than half went for 25 community airport projects in the western provinces. In the current fiscal year we have approved more that $1,800,000 for 24 projects, of which
Transportation. Policy
more than $1 million is earmarked for 15 airports in western Canada. That is not lip service.
The hon. member's motion also singles out Prince Rupert as a port that should be utilized to a greater degree. I am sure he will be pleased to hear that the government is in full accord with that aspect of it. In the spring of 1972 Prince Rupert became a National Harbours Board port. It is a large harbour, free of ice, and about 500 miles closer to the Orient than any other western port, which in itself illustrates the vital role it can play in the economy of western Canada.
The port of Prince Rupert will be developed not only in a manner which will be compatible with other west coast ports but in a manner which will be compatible with other modes of transportation. With this objective in mind we are working very closely with the British Columbia government. We now have agreement in principle on a joint transportation development program for northern British Columbia. The official position of the government of British Columbia is that it welcomes the new framework of federal-provincial co-operation and is particularly responsive to this set of new initiatives undertaken with the federal Department of Transport.
The joint program embraces railway, port and highway development. An extensive construction plan for a rail system jointly financed by the federal government and the British Columbia government is envisaged. The two governments agree that a comprehensive joint program for port development in Prince Rupert, including the location, size, type and timing, general cargo and bulk commodity terminal facilities and port authority or port commission operating arrangements will be required as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the Minister of Transport spoke about the regulatory function which is carried out by the Canadian Transport Commission. Since I believe this organization is quite often unjustly maligned, I should like to speak for a moment about its history, its responsibilities and some of its present-day activities. The Canadian Transport Commission was established in 1967 by the National Transportation Act. The act itself was meant to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada. Section 3 of the National Transportation Act defines the national transportation policy and states thatan economic, efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost is essential to protect the interests of the users of transportation and to maintain the economic well-being and growth of Canada.
This implies research, economic studies, constant adjustments due to changing conditions, and regulations designed to protect users of transportation. Numerous studies have been conducted by the economic, research and analytical units of the CTC to deal with subjects pertaining to all modes of transport-rail, air, water, commodity pipelines and extraprovincial motor vehicle transport. In 1972, for instance, there were studies on air services in the Strait of Bell Isle; three cases involving Arctic air service were the subject of hearings and a general review of air service in northwestern Quebec was carried

June 19, 1973

out. These are all areas of growth where transportation plays an important role.

speechtext:
Not your researchers; they are not capable.
Also in the field of air transport, the commission has recently revised its air carrier regulations and introduced new charter regulations because of changing requirements. Such regulations, because of international implications, are under constant review. To protect the public interest the commission makes thorough investigations before issuing licences to air carriers and has an extensive inspection program.
Activities of the commission with respect to rail operations and railway safety have increased considerably since the commission was created in 1967. In the public interest, the railways have been directed to continue operating a number of uneconomic passenger train services and branch lines, in which case they received subsidies. Two major decisions taken by the railway transport committee in this regard dealt with continuance of the Montreal-Toronto-Vancouver services and the Montreal-maritimes operations. The rationalization of these uneconomic services is under study.
An order in council was passed in 1967-which many members on the other side forget-to guarantee until January 1, 1975, the operation of 6,274 miles of branch lines in the prairie provinces. During the guarantee period the railways are prohibited from applying for abandonment. Since 1967 the commission has issued decisions on 61 applications for passenger train discontinuance. Only in 11 cases was discontinuance approved. No discontinuance has taken place without public hearings in the area affected. Thus far the railway transport committee has concentrated its efforts on the analysis of passenger train services, and only a few minor branch line abandonments have been approved to date.
Railway safety is given special attention by the commission. All accidents are investigated and inquiries are held in major cases to establish the cause of the accident and help prevent future accidents of the same nature. In addition, a special task force has been formed to study the movement of dangerous commodities. An advisory committee on railway safety, which includes representatives from the railways and the Canadian Railway Labour Association, has also been established.
At this juncture I should also like to point out that of all the railways operating in Canada and the United States, in 1971-which are the latest statistics available-the Canadian Pacific Railway ranked first and Canadian National Railways ranked fourth as having the fewest accidents.
In the field of domestic water transport, substantial subsidies have been granted to help ferry services throughout Canada. With regard to international maritime activities, advances in shipping together with related port facilities to serve the new generation of ships have sparked new interest in the economic and commercial bases on which shipping services are offered.

The extraprovincial motor vehicle transport committee has given aid to carriers under the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act. In 1972, close to $2 million was paid to truckers transporting goods from the Maritimes to markets in central and western Canada, and $8 million went to carriers operating within the Atlantic region. So the trucking business is also being subsidized. In addition, a major survey of the surface transportation system in Newfoundland has been undertaken, including operations of Newfoundland ferry and steamship services, transportation to Magdalen Islands and other policy recommendations.
The Canadian Transport Commission is stepping up its activities in all fields of transportation in order to discharge its mandate as set out in the National Transportation Act. In short, Mr. Speaker, I think the Canadian Transport Commission is doing an admirable job on a national and regional basis to ensure that the Canadian public and the industrial base of our country is served with a transportation system which is responsive, but at the same time subsidized only where a demonstrable need is evident.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks I think it is necessary for me to comment on the remarks which were made this afternoon about the aerospace industry in Winnipeg and Air Canada's overhaul facilities in Montreal. In so far as Winnipeg is concerned, there is no evidence which indicates that the viability of its aerospace industry is in question. On the contrary, the recent awarding of Air Canada contracts in Winnipeg, coupled with the aggressive sales programs, indicate that this Winnipeg industry is on the upswing. We are not even talking now about what we have given to save the aerospace industry and also BOAC. This is something which I hope the opposition will give us a chance to speak on at a later date.
With respect to allegations made about Air Canada's overhaul base, the corporation is confident that this facility is one of the most modern, best equipped and best staffed in the world with the best employees it can have. portation were initiated with the Atlantic premiers covering such areas as rail, trucking and the Darling report.

I might say that while the Conservatives were in power in 1962 they had many members from western Canada and never at any time did they try to implement a transportation policy, or any policy, anywhere else or in western Canada. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate because I think that a voice from the hills or mountains of British Columbia should be allowed to speak for that great disadvantaged area of Canada, the interior of B.C. which is serviced by the CNR and CPR. That is an area from which these companies have been allowed to, or have attempted to extract whatever the traffic would bear.
The B.C. government is the owner of a railway with which it services a large part of the interior of B.C. I am sure it has proved beyond a shadow of doubt that it has done a great service to the people. It has proved, as well, that it is possible to run a railway in an efficient manner and provide good service, without large amounts of subsidy.

speechtext: Did you hear that, Joe? Pay attention.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED URGENT NEED FOR A NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Those to my left are trying to take credit for this, but it was undertaken by a government that was in power long before the one they support. That was the government that supported independence and free enterprise. I do not know whether the present government will carry this on. I only hope that the people in power now will be able to do as good a job.
We must, in our marketing of B.C. fruits in the Okanagan, ship an average of 34 cars of fruit per day, six days a week for ten months of the year. Negotiations with the railways in regard to freight rates were long, tedious and frustrating before we had highways for trucks. Let us not forget that the B.C. fruit industry has no close markets, so this is really an export deal out of the valley. Vancouver, the closest large market, is 300 miles away by road and takes only about 15 per cent of the apple crop.
Before the Hope-Princeton highway opened up a truck route to Vancouver and the Rogers pass opened up a truck route to the prairie provinces we had many trials and tribulations in freight rate negotiations. I have seen carloads of apples sent to Winnipeg, unloaded, put in storage then reloaded at a later date and sent to a destination in Florida. A rebate was given with respect to the total, over-all freight rate. It was much cheaper to haul over the American railways than the Canadian railways.
We used such gimmicks as trucking fruit across the border, loading it on American carriers, hauling by them
4920

June 19, 1973
Transportation Policy
to a border point just below Winnipeg, unloading on to trucks again and hauling it up to Winnipeg by truck again, all at a lower cost than shipping directly by Canadian rail. We did this before we received any recognition and a better freight rate. Now that trucking has become an established fact, the big rail companies have effectively also become the big truck carriers, to the point that one wonders if we have any real competition today. We had to use such gimmicks in order to get an effective rail rate. This is what we had to do in that area. I do not think that was fair. I think our predicament should have been recognized and we should not have had to do that sort of thing.
In the past few years there has been a constant shortage of rail cars to haul fruit. The fruit growers get more agitated about this when they find, at Japanese orange time, that although they are suffering from a greater shortage there is no shortage of cars to haul Japanese oranges which are in direct competition with them. The latest development in the changeover from reefer cars to mechanical cars has meant that most of the CNR-built cars are not big enough to take the minimum tariff weight of 46,000 pounds as determined by the Trans-Continental Fruit Bureau whose headquarters are in Chicago and of which the CNR is a member. The CNR also wants to specify routings via the Niagara frontier, or eastern gateways. I suppose this is good business on their part, and their service is good up to these points of entry. However, the service on the American carrier or connecting lines is lousy. These lines have attempted this route and are requesting routings through Chicago where the service is excellent.
British Columbia fruit growers are in the business of producing apples for sale. Their best returns come from the grades of apples they sell to the United States. This adds to the balance of trade and exports for Canada-a balance, incidentally, which is very heavily weighted in foodstuffs coming into Canada from the United States. I certainly do not believe it is wrong to expect Canadian transportation companies, especially the government-owned CNR, to co-operate in these endeavours.
The lumber industry of British Columbia has for some months been faced with a shortage of cars to haul their products for export. Two or three weeks ago I was fortunate to be able to sit in at a meeting of the Canadian lumber industry. They had a panel on transportation. I was amazed to hear representatives from the CNR and CPR tell these people how lucky they were. They pointed out that they were operating their business to make a profit. It appeared to me that they did not care whether the lumber industry had cars to export their products or not. It is necessary to have extra cars if we are to have a balance of trade and efficiently move our produce and products. The transportation companies have an obligation to these people, but they seemingly do not think they have to be a part of what we do in Canada.
The situation in the lumber industry is similar to that of the fruit industry. They just have not been able to get the proper types of cars. They are trying to tell the people to rent these cars. In order to do so they would have to go to an American carrier. They would like these people to rent them, use them for their products and use the Canadian

rail system. This is not the type of thing that should happen in this country. We should be supplying the proper cars. After all, we own the railway. We should at least provide the facilities for the movement of our produce and products. All of the industry, especially in the interior of British Columbia, is having transportation problems where this philosophy prevails of getting all that the traffic will bear. This applies to goods coming in as well as goods being shipped out.
I recently received a letter from one of my constituents. He informed me that the cost of shipping pianos into the Okanagan had increased by 100 per cent. Checking up on this, I find it was an easy "out" for the railways; they had just changed their rate structure and there was nothing people could do about it.
I should like to say a few words about air traffic. The railroads have gradually been forgetting how to transport people. They made the service worse and worse until the people moved away from them, and now all we have is air traffic. One of the areas in my riding, Grand Forks, designated a site for industrial development. There has been nothing done to improve facilities for air traffic. The city council of Grand Forks has provided an excellent park for industrial expansion, at reasonable cost. The people there are able and ready to work, the climate is excellent and the district is ideally situated as a place where people can enjoy a good quality of life. The airport is well situated to serve the whole of the south central, interior region. However, the job is only half done and too many airplanes have to fly over the airport in the fall and winter months because of low weather ceilings.
This could easily be avoided through the installation of a proper beacon system, and action should be taken immediately in my opinion. In the heat of summer, some planes have to fly over because the runways are too short. Land suitable for extension is there, and this should be used. We designate an area as one for industrial expansion but we do not provide the transport facilities necessary to make it work.
I should like to put on record some interesting figures in connection with Kelowna airport. The population in the area it serves increased at a rate of 6M* per cent between 1966 and 1971, while the total population growth of British Columbia amounted to 3.2 per cent in the same period. In Canada as a whole it was 1 Vi per cent. Airport use increased by 360 per cent between 1966 and 1972, from 26,726 passengers in 1966 to 108,000 in 1972. By 1981 it is expected that the annual rate of movement by air will be 250,000. This illustrates the need for larger aircraft in order to provide increased capacity with economy. Therefore, the runway must be extended. This should be done as soon as possible before the growth pattern around the airport becomes such that people will resist an extension.
An instrument landing system is a necessity in order to reduce the inconvenience caused by cancelled flights and to provide added safety for operations carried on within existing limits. There is great potential for air freight generated by products of the Okanagan, especially fresh fruits.
June 19, 1973

I was surprised to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) refer to Air Canada this afternoon as a sacred cow. I quite often travel across Canada by Air Canada. I apologize to Your Honour. That is a slip I do not usually make. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for St. Boniface about Prince Rupert. I really appreciate the attention he gave to that port. I was delighted to hear him refer to the fact that we in Prince Rupert are 500 miles closer to the Orient than is Vancouver, and to hear all the other things he said about the possibilities and potential of Prince Rupert. However, I recall that same speech being reproduced in the Prince Rupert News when Mackenzie King was there in 1919.
May I also say that the attention that has been paid to the port of Prince Rupert was not the result of any deliberate act on the part of the federal government but was a response to long years of hard work by the people of the city of Prince Rupert, the port development commission, and others including my predecessor, the late Ted Apple-whaite, a member of this chamber before I got here. He did much to gain respect for this particular port, and no credit for this is due either to this government or to the hon. member for St. Boniface. However, I am glad to hear that he now recognizes that this port does exist.
With respect to his comments about the development of the railways in the north and the relationship that exists between the Canadian National Railway and the B.C. Railway, this came about as a result of the direct, conscious, deliberate initiative that was taken by the current government of British Columbia. May I say thank you, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the government and to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) for replying to this initiative which has been taken by our provincial government in B.C., which after all is how these things come about.
May I say a few words with respect to the western economic conference which is to take place in July in Calgary. One of the subject matters of this conference will undoubtedly be transportation. According to comments made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Transport and other cabinet ministers, this is a grand move on the part of this government; it has now recognized the situation in the west and has prompted and promoted this western economic conference. Let me tell the government, Mr. Speaker, that this initiative did not come from them; the initiative came from October 30 last. All that this government is doing is responding to that initiative taken by the people of the west who have been neglected too long. This is simply a belated, long overdue recognition of the disenchantment of westerners for years with activities centred here in Ottawa and controlled in eastern Canada.
I would not say this had it not been that my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) is prompting me from the wings. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who also purports to be a westerner, almost blew the conference with his intemperate remarks the other day, but I was glad to see during the question period today, although he tried his best to wriggle out of it, that be finally admitted his error.

Let me say something about transportation as it affects northern B.C. Transportation is crucial to our survival and our development. Without it the whole area will stagnate. It is crucial to our communications. It is vital to the decision whether or not northern British Columbia will develop further and become a viable part of the nation.
We are involved with three forms of transportation, rail, air and water. In different parts of northern B.C. there are different involvements, none greater or lesser than the others, depending on the area affected. As I said earlier, the development of rail transportation in that area as a co-operative concept between the federal and provincial governments has been brought into focus by the initiatives taken by Bob Williams, the B.C. minister of lands, Premier Barrett, and others of that calibre, and as talks continue we are very hopeful of a favourable outcome. Fortunately the Minister of Justice is not involved, at least as far as I know, in these discussions.
I have had discussions about the matter with the Minister of Transport and our discussions have been warm, friendly and considerate. I have also had discussions with the people in the government of British Columbia, and as I say we are hopeful that something really worth while will emerge from these discussions as a result of a co-operative spirit which heretofore has not existed.
I do not want to be partisan about this, but unfortunately there is a political taint so far as Prince Rupert is concerned inasmuch as the Liberal government follows the line that northern resources should be shipped out of northern ports. I for one reject that concept. The purpose of transportation should not be to milk the country dry of its natural resources and ship them out to some other land or country for processing; surely the purpose of developing a port is to have it serve as a two-way street. We should try to develop the port of Prince Rupert so we can ship out finished products manufactured in British Columbia, thus providing the people of the province with employment centred around the resources of the area.
I should like to speak for a moment or two about air transportation, with which we are vitally concerned. How many airstrips exist in the area that I represent in northern B.C.? I do not know. I have not counted them, but there must be 50 or 60. These are largely small gravel strips which serve relatively small communities. In other words, they are the type of airstrips that would be eligible for a grant from, I believe it is the local airport development fund administered by the Department of Transport to assist in grading and paving small airstrips and the construction of administrative buildings.
In the fund this year there is $2 million, an insignificant, piddling amount of money for the work that remains to be done. This money is doled out, to start with, by a very stingy minister. Last year the department had a different minister and $3 million was allocated to the fund in the estimates, but of course last year was an election year. In any event, as I have said, $2 million is not a very significant amount.
Recently a presentation was made to the minister by three municipalities which combined together, Port St. James, Vanderhoof and Burns Lake. These communities made a very worth-while presentation to the minister outlining the need for development assistance for the
June 19, 1973

three airports in those communities. They asked for the sum of $625,000 as a contribution toward the development of those airports.
Do you know how much $625,000 is, Mr. Speaker? To me it is a lot of money. I see you are shaking your head, and doubtless it is a lot of money to you and to people in the Maritimes. If I were to stack that amount of money on my desk I would not know how much room it would take up. I know how much $3,000 is; it buys me a car, and that figure does have some meaning. But one thing I do know is that $625,000 is only one five-hundredth of 1 per cent of the total amount of money the minister has in his hands for airport development. And I did not get Statistics Canada to work that figure out for me, either. Yet we can get none of this money, or relatively little. That impinges upon the potential development of that area.
Fort St. James is a relatively small community in the frontier area of northern British Columbia. It was the place that the late Grant McConachie, who founded Canadian Pacific Airlines, lived in, operated out of and flew out of. It was the community in which Russ Baker, founder of Pacific Western Airlines, lived in and flew out of in the early days. That is the area which is the jumping off spot for air travel for great distances northward.
Vanderhoof is 50 or 60 miles away. There was an airport built there during World War II and it served a good purpose at that time. As far as the federal government is concerned, it has had relatively little purpose since then. That airport at Vanderhoof has been maintained for the last 25 or 30 years by the village and municipality of Vanderhoof.

-the village of Vanderhoof was able to keep pace with airport needs only by going considerably beyond the requirements of the lease agreement. The cost of all this was borne entirely by the village and municipality of Vanderhoof. They received no help from this $2 million fund. I give full credit to the mayor of Vanderhoof, Everett Stevens, who was the Conservative candidate in Skeena during the last federal election and will be again whenever the next election takes place. He has done a tremendous job in trying to push the needs of that area before the federal government and I wish him continued success in his activities in that regard.
The Burns Lake airport also serves an area with some
7,000	or 8,000 people. The airport has had some recent improvements. From January 1 of this year to the end of April, 400 airline tickets were sold to people in the Burns

Lake area to travel on aircraft that stop at the airstrip at Burns Lake. These are the things that have happened, and these are the things which have largely been ignored.
When it comes to water transportation, the coastal area is served primarily by Northland Shipping. It receives a subvention from the water transport committee of the Canadian Transport Commission. I do not know the reason, but the Canadian Transport Commission is currently undertaking an investigation of Northland Shipping and that subvention or subsidy. I hope it is for the purpose of making clear the need for water transportation along the north coast of British Columbia, and not for the purpose of finding ways and means of driving Northland Shipping or any other shipping company out of business. I hope this is not a political question.
I am sorry I cannot give any accolades to the Canadian Transport Commission, as other hon. members, including the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), have done. I think that organization is a monstrosity. It was conceived by a gentleman who used to be in this House and wanted to find a haven for himself-Jack Pickersgill. It was not conceived for the purpose of trying to develop-

There are only a few minutes left, Mr. Speaker, and if anyone had said no it would probably have been myself; but I was silent for a change. I had pretty well reached the end of my remarks. I was saying, in respect of the Canadian Transport Commission and its various committees, that it seems their primary function has been to serve their bureaucratic intentions and propensities rather than the people they are supposed to serve. Very unfortunately, this is the outgrowth and development of that type of bureaucracy which is aloof and immune almost from parliamentary inquiry, and aloof and immune almost from ministerial authority or question. It is just an agency governed by itself, circumscribed by its own concepts. We can find dozens of instances where the needs of people in all parts of this land, in terms of transportation by air, water, rail or truck have been stifled because of lack of action, response, consideration and concern by the Canadian Transport Commission.
You bet we need a transportation policy in this nation, Mr. Speaker. The first step we can take toward obtaining such a national transportation policy, if the government is reluctant, is to dismember and disband the Canadian Transport Commission and start from scratch, and I am sure we could do a damn sight better job.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOUTH AFRICA-REASON COMMONWEALTH TARIFF PREFERENCE NOT WITHDRAWN BY CANADA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOUTH AFRICA-REASON COMMONWEALTH TARIFF PREFERENCE NOT WITHDRAWN BY CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at page 4256 of Hansard 1 am reported as having asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question in respect of this subject matter as follows:
In view of the fact South Africa has been expelled from the Commonwealth of Nations for some time now, would the Prime Minister tell the House why no plans were ever formulated by his government to withdraw Commonwealth preferential tariff treatment from that country?
The Prime Minister's answer was less than satisfactory, hence my representations tonight. The Canadian govern-
IThe Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
ment some time ago in its publication "Foreign Policy for Canadians" was outspoken in its condemnation of the character of the white regime in South Africa, stating that the Portuguese territories are essentially a manifestation of an outdated colonialism, that South Africa is possessed by the cancer of apartheid, and that southwest Africa and Rhodesia have elements of both.
In support of this, in 1964 the Canadian government refused the sale of paramilitary trucks by the Ford Motor Company of Canada to South Africa. In 1968 and 1969 Canada supported strong resolutions at the United Nations condemning continued Portuguese rule over its African colonies and supporting the right of the people of Angola and Mozambique to independence and self-determination. Canada voted against the continued authority of South Africa over Namibia, formerly southwest Africa, and committed itself to mandatory economic sanctions against Rhodesia.
In further support of this policy, in June, 1970, the Government of Canada agreed to ensure that Polymer, at that time a Crown corporation, divest itself of equity holdings in a South African company. However, this apparently Liberal trend in our African policy has not been sustained. Lately we have shied away from giving moral support to independent African countries which have been decrying the policies of the oppressive white regime.
In direct contrast to this, the Minister of External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) gave open support to the principle of dialogue with South Africa, a principle which since has lost almost totally its initial rather hesitant backing from a few black African countries. Further to this, we have also continued to extend to the Republic of South Africa the Commonwealth preference tariff agreement, although South Africa left the Commonwealth in 1961.
The conclusion is unavoidable that the Canadian government in recent years has reversed its position in regard to South Africa. The reason for a softening government position toward racial oppressive regimes in South Africa is not easily discernible. Certainly nothing has happened in South Africa itself to warrant this reduced sensitivity toward the emerging independent nations on that continent. Indeed, had the Canadian government been more responsive to the growing awareness among private individuals and organizations in Canada of the developing crisis in South Africa, it clearly would have treated more seriously and responsively our foreign policy toward that area.
Instead, Ottawa has chosen to adopt a more cautious approach to the problem, a response that clearly favoured what the government perceived to be Canada's business interest. The government may also have been misled by a poorly done, ill-informed analysis of the situation in South Africa and thus was prompted in its policies by faulty observation and poor interpretation of African concerns.
Could it be argued that the considerable post-war expansion of foreign investment has contributed to a liberalization of racist policies in South Africa? Has this economic growth helped to narrow the economic gap between white and black conditions in South Africa? Has
June 19, 1973

it contributed to dramatically improved living standards of the black citizen? Can it be argued that foreign investment and economic growth has led to an undermining of apartheid. The only answer is an emphatic no. By giving Commonwealth preferential tariff treatment to this country we are prolonging the day when apartheid, the scourge of the civilized world, will be nothing but a faint memory in the minds of all the peoples of the world.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOUTH AFRICA-REASON COMMONWEALTH TARIFF PREFERENCE NOT WITHDRAWN BY CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe is forgetting a major fact in the discussion of our trade relations: namely that the latter's purpose is not to strengthen or approve the political regimes with which we have trade relations.
If that were the case, I can assure the House that our trade relations would change very often. If, for example, Canada were to condemn dictatorship or any other nondemocratic system, it would have trade relations with much fewer countries than at present.
The other point I would like to stress, is that South Africa was never expelled from the Commonwealth; it of course withdrew. But a more important fact is that the Commonwealth has never been asked to abandon the preferential tariff which this country has with the other members of the Commonwealth, unlike Rhodesia, for example, with whom Canada broke off all relations, in order to respect the resolutions of the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.
I would also like to remind the hon. member that Canada is preparing for a thorough review of all these tariff agreements in the near future, by means of, among other things, the new round of GATT negotiations.
Finally, I would remind the hon. member that Canada has agreed to establish in the near future, preferential tariffs for the developing countries.
That is in the main, Mr. Speaker, my reply to the well-founded question put by the hon. member. I would like to remind him one last time that the question of preferential tariffs has worked in the past, and continues to do so, in favour of the Canadian economy.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SHIPMENT OF HORSES TO EUROPE FOR . SLAUGHTER-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ELIMINATE
AGRICULTURE-SHIPMENT OF HORSES TO EUROPE FOR . SLAUGHTER-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ELIMINATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago during the question period in this chamber I raised a subject which I consider to represent a disgrace to Canada, that is, the cruel shipment of horses from this country overseas to Europe, for slaughter there and to be consumed as horsemeat. I asked on that occasion:
Having in mind the fact that the cruel trade involving the shipment of Canadian horses by sea for slaughter in Europe has started again in the face of strong representations against it by all the humane societies in Canada, will the minister look into this situation with a view to stopping this unfortunate situation?
The minister replied that he had asked his department to carry out a study, that he had received some reports, and he added some other words about the regulations covering the horses prior to their shipment. I was not
Adjournment Debate
satisfied with that reply, and neither are the people in the humane societies in Canada. All across this country there is a great deal of concern about this situation.
In the few minutes permitted to me during this period I can do no better than quote from a letter which the minister's office received, and of which I have a copy, from Mr. Tom Hughes who is general manager of the Ontario Humane Society and also vice-president of the Animal Welfare Federation of Canada. He wrote this letter following the exchange between the minister and myself and in it he said:
Dear Mr. Whelan,
I have just received a copy of Hansard in which you were reported replying to a question from Mr. Mather concerning the export of live horses to Europe. In view of the nature of your reply to Mr. Mather I felt I should write to you.
Your department has consistently stated that it is the policy of the government that horses will only be exported to Europe for "work or breeding." This requirement is totally ignored by the European importers and even ridiculed. We have reliable proof from observers, who we arranged to meet the horses in Europe, that horses are being sent straight to the Paris slaughterhouses.
In your reply to Mr. Mather you stated that the horses "must be preconditioned, their age must be known and it must be known whether or not they are pregnant before they are loaded on the ship". I can only say with great respect, I am quite convinced that your department does not have this information.
Preconditioning can only mean that the animal is kept for some period of time at some location in Canada and brought into good condition in the normal way before being shipped. This is simply not the case. Horses are coming into Montreal and Saint John from various points in the United States and Canada without any attempt being made to precondition them. Our inspectors are watching these animals go through Ontario. The dealers are well known to us and we observe the horses from time to time both on route on the roads or in the sales barns.
I should interject at this point, Mr. Speaker: it is not in Mr. Hughes' letter, but I know this is his information as well, that the United States does not permit the shipment of horses overseas for slaughter in the quantities involved here. They do not permit the shipment of horses for slaughter overseas. The letter continues:
Another matter which is of great concern to the society-
That is the Ontario Humane Society.
-is that the veterinary inspection, which is being established in Montreal both by representatives of the health of animals branch and the veterinarians employed by the Canadian SPCA, are now apparently being avoided by shipping the horses through Saint John, New Brunswick. Only a few days ago the Holstein Express left for Europe with 400 horses aboard. I am quite sure that these horses were not given the veterinary inspection they would have received in Montreal.
Apart from the conditions on board ship, there is the unnecessary strain and stress to which these horses are subjected on the long journey across the United States and Canada, there is the strain and stress involved in the repeated loadings and unloadings, there is the stress to which they are subjected in the transportation across to Europe and finally there is the undeniable fact that they may not be slaughtered humanely in the European slaughterhouses. We recognize that the Government of Canada has no control over conditions in Europe so therefore, with the best will in the world, there is nothing the Canadian government can do to protect the horses from this abuse. The only solution is to abolish the export of live horses for slaughter and to avoid the farcical suggestion that all the horses are going for "work"-
A tragic suggestion, Mr. Speaker.

June 19, 1973
Adjournment Debate -abolish the export for work as well.
The horses, if they are to be killed for horse meat purposes, should be killed in Canada. The letter ends:
We urge you to intervene in this matter and take the appropriate action.
This concludes the letter from Mr. Hughes. I can only say that I agree with it entirely, and with the humane movement in Canada which urges that the Canadian government take steps to end what is a disgrace to our country and which is not permitted by the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SHIPMENT OF HORSES TO EUROPE FOR . SLAUGHTER-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ELIMINATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture shares the concern of the hon. member with regard to the humane treatment of animals. In the last few years, the Department of Agriculture has done much to reduce to a minimum the possibilities of cruelty to horses shipped by sea to Europe. In the fall of 1970, steps were taken, under the act on the shipping of animals, to suspend shipments during the winter months. The shipping season now extends from April 1 to October 31. A few trial shipments were allowed with preliminary inspection and the presence of a department veterinarian. As a result of those experiments, health standards were incorporated into the regulation on the shipment of live animals. In short, those standards require a 7 to 10 day pre-conditioning period around the port of loading, that the horses be less than 11 years old, in good condition and free from sickness, and that the mares not be in a state of advanced pregnancy, and that a veterinarian accompany any shipment of more than 25 horses.
The hon. member might be interested in a few statistics resulting from the application of those standards. On August 17, 1971, 540 horses were shipped, and none died. On September 20, 1971, 510 horses were shipped, and none died. On November 3, 1971, 800 horses were shipped, and none died. On May 2, 1972, 293 horses were shipped and five died. On May 5, 1972, 416 horses were shipped, and three died. On June 18, 1972, 220 horses were shipped and two died. On August 19, 1972, 317 horses were shipped, and one had to be put away. On September 29, 1972, 326 horses were shipped, and two died, one having to be put away. On April 27, 1973, 150 were shipped, and one died, the cause of death not being attributable to the voyage. In short, Mr. Speaker, the mortality rate has been 0.4 p. 100 since the implementation of the preventive measures, whereas it had been 7.3 p. 100 before the summer of 1971.

HEALTH-STEPS TO COUNTERACT INCREASE IN CIGARETTE SMOKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising this evening to speak on the subject of cigarette consumption. I asked my question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and his answer was not satisfactory, probably because he did not have the necessary time. I am particularly concerned by the increase in the consumption of cigarettes; it has increased by about 5 per cent. At the same time, we have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars of the taxpayers'

money to prevent this increase. The question obviously is: Are we doing the job that we tried to do some years ago?
I first became interested in this problem and aware of it over 20 years ago, in about 1948. Doctor Walter Ochsner, one of the greatest chest surgeons of his time and a great cancer expert who used to work in New Orleans, had a dictum. If you had a cough, had a shadow, and had smoked cigarettes for 20 years, you were suffering from cancer unless you could prove differently. I think that dictum holds true today. This is a serious matter.
The minister said that he would investigate the age groups involved in the consumption of cigarettes. He wanted to know in which group the increase was taking place and whether young people were becoming increasingly addicted to smoking. To date we have not heard any answer on this matter. True, the direct threat of the minister's predecessor did have some effect in that cigarette manufacturers stopped advertising on radio and television and also put warning signs and words in all their newspaper advertising. Despite all this, advertising is on the increase. In last Monday's Gazette, as hon. members may recall, there was a report of a lady complaining about her teenage children seeing advertising. In the Canadian Weekend magazine there were five pages of cigarette advertising.

speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: HEALTH-STEPS TO COUNTERACT INCREASE IN CIGARETTE SMOKING
speechtext:
It appears that the present minister will not carry on, or will not support the thrust of the proposed legislation that was not passed when his predecessor was responsible for that portfolio. That the situation is very serious no one will deny. There are probably seven million cigarette smokers in Canada. One asks, what value has the taxpayer received for the hundreds of thousands of dollars spent in the anti-smoking campaign? What value have we received for that money, and how many people have been deterred from smoking?
Cancer of the lung is one of the fastest increasing cancers of the present day. Over 4,000 people annually die from it. Once it is established it is very hard to cure. Statistically, three-quarters of those cases are associated with cigarette smoking. Coronary artery disease and arteriosclerosis occur much more frequently in those who smoke cigarettes. Emphysema becomes much worse with smoking. Invariably, the smoking of cigarettes is a prime cause in chronic bronchitis. I could go on listing these diseases. Smoking also detrimentally affects anyone with Berger's disease, and so on. All these diseases and many others are caused or aggravated in many cases by cigarettes. The findings in this respect are well substantiated. I will put this passage on the record:
Premature deaths and disabling illnesses caused by cigarette smoking have now reached epidemic proportions and present the most challenging of all opportunities for preventive medicine in this country.
That is a report of the Royal College of Physicians of Britain. I wish to put another quotation on the record as follows:
Cigarette smoking is the most important cause of chronic obstructive broncho-pulmonary disease in the United States. Ciga-
June 19, 1973

rette smoking increases the risk of dying from pulmonary emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
Cigarette smoking is a significant risk factor contributing to the development of coronary heart disease, including fatal coronary heart disease and its most severe expression, sudden and unexpected death.
Cigarette smoking is the main cause of lung cancer in men. Cigarette smoking is a cause of lung cancer in women but accounts for a smaller proportion of the cases than in men.
This quotation is from "The Health Consequences of Smoking", a report of the Surgeon General of the United States public health service, 1971. This proves the case, if it needs any proof or reminder. What is the record here? Instead of practising preventive medicine we are treating the sick. We are looking after people after they have the disease. We are locking the barn door after the horse has been stolen. We are increasing our health costs tremendously instead of preventing them. I suspect this is the reason the Minister of National Health and Welfare wanted to give provincial governments all the money they could get from taxing tobacco and alcohol.
He would turn the federal taxes over in toto if he could just walk out of this shared-cost program with the provinces. That was a great mistake. The provinces were already starting to cut back on services. He must get out before it gets worse. He, like Pontius Pilate, wanted to wash his hands-or did the minister feel guilty about this tax coming from sources that were causing so much misery?
The problem is what to do about this situation. The minister, if I interpret him correctly, believes in education. If that is it, and that is preventive medicine, let's get going on it. Would the minister state how much has been spent of the moneys allotted to research? How much money have the cigarette companies funded into finding a safe cigarette? How much money does the Department of Agriculture spend in subsidizing the tobacco interests?
Finally, how can we substantially reduce the respiratory and cardiovascular diseases that cause not only death but chronic illness and add tremendously to our cost of health care which is threatening to cause a cut in medical services? That is the problem. It will not rest until positive action is taken.

Mr. Speaker, the Department of National Health and Welfare is indeed concerned about

the hazards of cigarette smoking, knowing as it does that two of the major diseases related to smoking, heart attack and lung cancer, are now the first and second causes of death for men aged 45 to 64. In addition, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths not only for men but for both sexes combined. Death rates are, of course, only the tip of the iceberg of these health problems and the department is concerned about attacking the problem from a number of angles, given the statistics which would indicate a levelling off of smoking among teenage boys but an increase among teenage girls.
In its continuing efforts to assist smokers to discontinue smoking, the department is experimenting with a new computerized technique entitled Health Hazard Appraisal, which, in providing motivational information about other risks to health besides smoking, encourages training sessions for those wishing to learn how to operate smoking withdrawal clinics.
New techniques of reaching young people are being experimented with, including the involvement of youth themselves in teaching about smoking and health, and consideration is being given to another youth conference on smoking and health, as well as our on-going production of educational materials, television spot announcements, films, posters, leaflets, teachers' guides, and so on.
In recognition of the continuation of smoking by many persons because of addiction, the department is co-operating with the Department of Agriculture in a program of research into less hazardous tobacco products. A laboratory is being built and equipped on the tobacco research station at Delhi, Ontario, as announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) on January 22, 1973. In addition, studies are being carried out at the University of Waterloo on the chemical and physical characterization of cigarette smoke.
Finally, the department is encouraging the progressive reduction of tar and nicotine levels in brands of cigarettes for sale in Canada. On February 21 of this year the Minister of National Health and Welfare published the tar and nicotine levels of the more widely available brands, and while encouraging the manufacturers to help bring these figures to public attention by stating them on cigarette packages, cartons and vending machines reiterated the department's position that it is safer not to smoke at all.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS OF MADAM INDIRA GANDHI PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA TO BOTH HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA ON TUESDAY, JUNE 19, 1973
speechtext: On behalf of senators and members of the House of Commons I call upon the Right Honourable the Prime Minister of Canada to introduce the Right Honourable the Prime Minister of India.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ADDRESS OF MADAM INDIRA GANDHI PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA TO BOTH HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA ON TUESDAY, JUNE 19, 1973
speechtext:
Madam Prime Minister of India, Madam Speaker of the Senate, Mister Speaker of the House of Commons, members of the Parliament of Canada.
On behalf of the people of Canada, and of their representatives from both Houses of Parliament, I bid you, Madam Prime Minister, a cordial welcome.
You, Madam, are not the first leader of your country to honour this institution with your presence, nor is this the first occasion that you have been introduced to the Parliament of Canada. Nevertheless your appearance in this place today does represent a "first" of a kind because the Prime Minister of India who preceded you here was that distinguished international statesman, your father, the late Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. In this chamber today are several parliamentarians who were present on that earlier occasion.

During the years since Prime Minister Nehru stood here, Canadian parliamentarians have seized many opportunities, both collectively and individually, to express their interest in India. An outstanding example is to be found in the career of a former speaker of this chamber who later represented Canada as High Commissioner to India before returning to this country to occupy his present high office of Governor General of Canada, ably seconded by his wife who is with us today. Another example is found in the friendship which has developed between the present Speakers of the House of Commons and the Lok Sabha. These gentlemen have visited and conferred with one another on several occasions in our two capitals.
Gathered in tnis chamber today to listen to your address, Madam Prime Minister, are men and women from every region of our widespread country. Their presence in this institution, and their activities here, are guided by the same great traditions of parliamentary practice familiar to you as an Indian parliamentarian. Those traditions and those practices we regard, as do you, as a priceless heritage and as an incomparable guarantee of democratic freedoms. They are among the many invisible bonds that link us
together as fellow members of that unique and immensely valuable association, the Commonwealth.
We share with you as well an appreciation of the problems that confront societies as diverse in their interests and their geographic roots as are those of Canada and India. We are aware, as are you, of the need to fulfill the expectations of peoples rightly demanding recognition of individual dignity and public well-being.
[ English]
Your visit to Canada comes a quarter of a century following India's political maturity as an independent nation state, but several thousand years following India's maturity as a rich and creative civilization. It is partly in gratitude for the immense legacy of art, of wisdom, of philosophy, which we in the west have received from your ageless nation, that Canadians have offered developmental assistance to the modern India. And we share your pride that India's long-recognized role as a major political participant in the international community will soon be matched by an equally important role as a major economic participant.
In our talks these past two days, Madam, we have been able to identify several areas in which the Indian-Canadi-an relationship, always a friendly one, has developed and matured. We now share an opportunity to engage our two countries in a new and equally beneficial pattern but one which is based not so much on aid as on trade, not so much on technical advice as on the exchange of experience. In this respect I regard your visit here as marking a milestone in the history of Indian-Canadian relations which is as important as that marked by the visit of Prime Minister Nehru in 1949. In his address here, Mr. Nehru said that Asia was renascent, that having gained political freedom, India faced the task of harnessing for human betterment her will, her natural resources, and her human material.
India's successes in doing so, and your personal contribution to those successes, Madam, not only prove the accuracy of that forecast but give to Canadians occasion to congratulate you on these accomplishments.
We welcome you, Madam Prime Minister, to this Parliament.
